# Top Tech News Today, September 18, 2026: Anthropic, Google, Meta, Nvidia, OpenAI & More

It’s Friday, September 18, 2026, and the last 24 hours made one thing hard to miss: AI is being handed real authority faster than anyone is locking the doors behind it. Nvidia’s Jensen Huang said the company expects to sell twice as many chips next year. OpenAI dropped a legal-research index spanning 230 million URLs. Apple let coding agents drive Safari. Google gave households a shared family agent. Europe moved to switch AI companions off for children by default.

Then came the warning signs. A tiny startup used Claude to reach OpenAI employee accounts. A “pinned” plugin became a zero-click backdoor across four coding agents. A compromised marketing script spread malicious code across more than 100,000 websites. Spain recorded its first data breach attributed to an autonomous agent. And three CEOs persuaded Washington to abandon an industry-funded AI referee.

Meanwhile, Anthropic is putting AI into a physical biology lab, Abu Dhabi is bringing agentic AI into executive government meetings, and researchers are showing how frontier models can compress sophisticated cyber operations from months into days.

The fight is no longer simply about whether AI works. It is about who gets to act, who gets to watch, and what happens when action comes before safeguards.

That tension runs through today’s biggest technology stories. AI is moving from something people consult to something that can experiment, coordinate, predict, attack, advise, and act — while governments and companies race to build the chips, quantum systems, security controls, and rules needed to keep up.

Here are the top [technology news](https://techstartups.com/category/latest-technology-news/) stories shaping that transition today.

## Google Launches CC, a Gemini-Powered AI Agent Built to Run Family Life

Google is testing a new AI agent called CC that can coordinate schedules, documents, email, reminders, forms, and shared household tasks for up to six family members. Unlike a standard Gemini conversation, CC gets its own Google account and can connect to information that household members explicitly choose to share. Users can route certain emails to the agent, interact with it through Google Chat, or give it access to a shared Drive folder containing invitations and documents. Each morning, CC can generate a shared “Your Day Ahead” briefing, update calendars, track unfinished tasks, create documents, and prefill forms such as school permission slips.

Google says each CC deployment runs in an isolated cloud environment using its Antigravity agent infrastructure and current Gemini models, including Gemini 3.8 Flash. Crucially, the agent can build shared memory about household preferences while maintaining limits around what information individual family members choose to expose. Google also says CC will seek confirmation before sending information outside the family group. For now, the experiment is limited to adults using personal Google accounts and is available through a waitlist. The product illustrates where consumer AI is heading: away from standalone prompts and toward persistent agents with memory, permissions, identity, and the ability to act across multiple services.

**Why It Matters:** Google is testing whether the next major consumer-AI interface is not another chatbot, but a persistent digital operator embedded in everyday household workflows.

**Source:** Ars Technica.

## Microsoft and OpenAI Copyright Fight Escalates After Newly Unredacted AI Training Filings

Newly unredacted material in The New York Times’ copyright litigation against Microsoft and OpenAI has exposed internal discussions that could intensify the legal fight over AI training data. According to material described in the plaintiffs’ court brief, Microsoft executives internally worried about the economic damage AI-generated answers could cause publishers, while OpenAI personnel discussed the increasingly substitutive nature of chatbot answers. Microsoft’s own data, according to the filing, showed Copilot-generated answers cutting click-through traffic to the Times by as much as 93% compared with traditional Bing search. TechCrunch cautioned that much of the new information comes from the plaintiffs’ brief while underlying exhibits remain sealed, meaning some excerpts lack their full original context.

The filings also allege large-scale use of publisher material in training datasets, including more than 91,000 copies of works from the Times, New York Daily News, and Center for Investigative Reporting in certain mid-training datasets. Another Common Crawl-derived dataset allegedly contained more than two million documents from nytimes.com. Those assertions have not yet settled the core legal question: whether training a model on copyrighted material qualifies as fair use. But the newly disclosed material could matter because fair-use disputes often turn partly on market substitution and economic harm. Microsoft and OpenAI did not respond to TechCrunch’s requests for comment on the newly disclosed material.

**Why It Matters:** The AI copyright battle is increasingly shifting from abstract arguments about training data to evidence about how AI products may affect the economic market for original content.

**Source:** TechCrunch.

## Meta Oversight Board Orders Removal of AI Deepfakes and Calls for Stronger Safeguards

Meta’s Oversight Board has ordered Facebook to remove two AI-generated videos after finding that the platform’s existing policies were insufficient in those cases. One video falsely depicted a Scottish Labor councilor making inflammatory remarks about refugees; another manipulated the image of a young Muslim campaign volunteer. The board concluded that the first violated Meta’s hateful-conduct rules and the second breached its bullying and harassment policies. It also said the material should have received stronger AI-related warnings and recommended policy changes affecting how high-risk manipulated content is labeled and distributed.

The quasi-independent board proposed nine changes, including reducing algorithmic distribution of material marked as high-risk AI content, introducing warning screens before users view some manipulated media, increasing penalties for accounts that repeatedly distribute deceptive deepfakes, and broadening Meta’s definition of unwanted manipulated imagery. The rulings illustrate a growing enforcement problem for social platforms: generative AI can create convincing fake speech or behavior at negligible cost, while content-review systems still have to determine context, intent, harm, and whether manipulation crosses an existing policy line. For platforms operating at Meta’s scale, labeling alone may prove insufficient if recommendation algorithms continue pushing misleading material to millions of users before moderation decisions are made.

**Why It Matters:** AI deepfakes are forcing social platforms to decide whether disclosure labels are enough or whether manipulated content also needs reduced distribution and tougher enforcement.

**Source:** The Guardian.

## OpenAI Employee Accounts Breached in Ethical Hack Powered by Rival AI Models

Security researchers at Hacktron AI compromised several OpenAI employees’ ChatGPT accounts during an authorized security investigation, demonstrating how generative AI is lowering the barrier to sophisticated offensive-security work. The researchers initially used Anthropic’s Claude to help exploit an attack path involving an OpenAI staff discussion forum running on Discourse. From there, they reached employee accounts and progressed far enough to make a harmless pull request against OpenAI code hosted on GitHub. Hacktron said it could access code but did not download it. The team reported the work through OpenAI’s bug-bounty program, and OpenAI said it had addressed the vulnerabilities.

The striking part is not simply that an AI company was hacked during security testing. Hacktron said AI compressed work that once might have required a well-resourced team and months of effort into days. The researchers reportedly used Claude during the initial attack and later relied heavily on OpenAI’s own GPT-5.6 Sol. That creates an increasingly unusual cybersecurity loop: advanced models are simultaneously targets, defensive tools, and offensive research assistants. As AI agents gain better coding, browsing, reasoning, and tool-use capabilities, security teams may need to assume attackers can automate larger portions of reconnaissance, exploit development, and attack-chain construction.

**Why It Matters:** AI is shrinking the time and expertise required to execute complex cyberattacks, forcing defenders to rethink security economics.

**Source:** The Guardian.

## Anthropic Says Claude Now Leads 26% of the Work Building Its Next AI Models

Anthropic says Claude is increasingly participating in the research required to build future versions of itself. According to the company, Claude led about 26% of its model research and development work by August, meaning it could complete most assigned tasks from a high-level prompt while remaining under human supervision. That figure was effectively zero in February. Anthropic also says roughly 90% of its research and development now involves some form of collaboration with Claude, although that broader category includes tasks performed under close human direction rather than autonomous research.

The distinction matters because claims that AI is “building itself” can easily outrun what the evidence actually shows. Anthropic says its models are not autonomously designing and training their successors. But the direction is notable: AI systems are taking on larger pieces of AI research themselves, potentially shortening the feedback loop between one model generation and the next. Anthropic disclosed that roughly 30,000 agents were performing research and engineering work as of August and has called for standardized industry metrics showing how much frontier-model development is being done by AI. The company argues that better public measurement is needed as systems move closer to forms of recursive improvement that could become harder for humans to supervise.

**Why It Matters:** The speed of AI development could accelerate sharply if frontier models become increasingly capable participants in the research that produces their successors.

**Source:** Associated Press.

## Nvidia CEO Says AI Chip Demand Will Double Sales Again in 2027

Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang told reporters on the sidelines of a King Charles III AI summit in Scotland that [the company expects to sell twice as many chips next year](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/17/nvidia-huang-ai-chip-guidance.html) as it does this year. Huang tied the forecast to what he described as broad, country-by-country demand, saying governments and companies in nearly every market where Nvidia operates want to invest in artificial intelligence. The comments landed a day after Nvidia shares rose more than 2 percent and as investors weighed whether the AI infrastructure cycle is cooling. Nvidia does not publish unit volumes, but Huang said last fall that the company had shipped 6 million Blackwell GPUs over four quarters. The portfolio now spans data-center Blackwell and Rubin GPUs, networking and optical silicon, CPUs, robotics and automotive processors, and the chip inside Nintendo’s Switch 2.

The forecast builds on an already aggressive financial outlook. Nvidia recently reported $96.2 billion in quarterly revenue, up 106 percent year over year, and has guided to about 70 percent growth in the fiscal year ending January 2028 — a figure that would imply roughly $673 billion in sales if supply holds. Management has separately said unconstrained customer demand points closer to a doubling, with high-bandwidth memory remaining the binding constraint through fiscal 2028. Huang used the same appearance to push back on calls for a slowdown in frontier-model development, arguing that unsafe products should not be released rather than that new laws are required. For startups building on Nvidia systems, the message is that the bottleneck is still silicon and memory, not a collapse in orders.

**Why It Matters**: Huang’s unit forecast keeps the AI capex debate centered on supply, not vanishing demand, and that is the variable that sets pricing power for chips, cloud capacity, and infrastructure startups.

**Source**: CNBC.

## Zuckerberg, Musk and Huang Press Trump to Kill Industry-Funded AI Regulator

Mark Zuckerberg, Elon Musk and Jensen Huang [separately urged President Donald Trump](https://techstartups.com/2026/09/17/zuckerberg-musk-and-jensen-huang-reportedly-lobbied-trump-to-halt-industry-funded-ai-regulator-plan/) in recent weeks to reject an industry-funded AI oversight body modeled on ideas floated by Google DeepMind chief Demis Hassabis, according to reporting that circulated Thursday. The proposed organization would have resembled a FINRA-style standards-and-supervision outfit for frontier models. The three executives argued that such a body would concentrate power in the hands of OpenAI, Anthropic and Google and raised questions about who would sit on it. White House officials have told other AI executives that building consensus inside the administration is difficult because opponents of tighter rules are calling Trump directly.

The lobbying landed in the same week that Anthropic’s Dario Amodei called for a slower pace of capability gains, with Sam Altman and Hassabis publicly aligning on the need for more caution while Huang and Zuckerberg opposed a pause. Trump has dismissed existential-risk warnings as a “hoax” and argued that heavy U.S. restrictions would give China an advantage. Huang said at Salesforce’s Dreamforce conference that existing product-liability and safety laws are enough: if a company is not confident in a system, it should not ship it. Musk has instead floated mutual audits in which rival labs test one another’s models. Startups that expected a single private-sector rulebook now face a split market: safety-focused labs pushing standards, and the largest platform and chip companies defending a lighter federal touch.

**Why It Matters**: The collapse of a shared industry regulator leaves AI policy dependent on personal access to the White House, raising the odds of uneven rules for labs, chipmakers, and the startups that build on both.

**Source**: TechStartups via The Wall Street Journal, Forbes

## Anthropic Quietly Builds Physical Biology Lab as AI Push Moves Into Drug Science

Anthropic has quietly established a wet lab in the San Francisco Bay Area, pushing its AI ambitions beyond computer simulations and into physical biological experiments. The company’s head of life sciences, Eric Kauderer-Abrams, confirmed the facility to Reuters, saying real-world laboratory work remains essential for testing biological ideas. Anthropic is also exploring how its Claude models could direct robotic lab equipment with limited human intervention, although the company says human oversight remains central. Anthropic clarified that the facility itself is not specifically a drug-discovery lab, but life sciences has become one of the company’s largest investment areas by headcount and resources.

The move is significant because frontier AI companies are beginning to cross the boundary between generating scientific hypotheses and physically testing them. Anthropic has already launched Claude Science, acquired Coefficient Bio, and works with pharmaceutical companies including Genentech, Bristol Myers Squibb, and Novo Nordisk. Its longer-term focus includes difficult or commercially neglected diseases, while the company says it does not plan to run clinical trials and does not want to compete directly with drugmakers. The larger question is whether AI labs can compress the experimental cycle itself by connecting models, robotics, laboratory instrumentation, and biological data into one system.

**Why It Matters:** AI is beginning to move from analyzing scientific data to participating directly in the physical process of experimentation.

**Source:** Reuters.

## AI Forecasting Startup Mantic Raises More Than $20M After Beating Human Forecasters

London-based ManticAI has raised more than $20 million after its forecasting system outperformed human participants in a major prediction competition. Sky News reported that Balderton Capital and Radical Ventures jointly led the financing, with Microsoft’s M12 venture fund also participating. The startup was co-founded by former Google DeepMind researcher Toby Shevlane and Ben Day and specializes in adapting frontier AI models to assign probabilities to future political, economic, business, and cultural events. Sky reported that the round was being raised at a valuation close to $90 million.

Mantic drew attention after its system performed strongly in the 2026 Metaculus forecasting competition, where AI systems collectively showed they could compete with — and in some cases outperform — experienced human forecasters. Forecasting represents an interesting next step for enterprise AI because the output is measurable: a system assigns probabilities, the event happens or does not, and performance can be scored over time. That makes forecasting potentially useful in markets, supply chains, risk management, strategic planning, and intelligence analysis. It also creates a tougher standard than fluent text generation because impressive language cannot compensate indefinitely for poor calibration. Commercial success, however, will depend on whether competition performance carries over reliably to messy real-world decisions.

**Why It Matters:** If AI forecasting continues improving, probabilistic prediction could become a new enterprise-AI category alongside coding, research, and data analysis.

**Source:** Sky News.

## France Opens Smart-Glasses Probe as AI Wearables Trigger New Privacy Backlash

French prosecutors have opened a criminal investigation into suspected sexual harassment involving smart glasses, while France’s data-protection authority is fielding complaints and questions from businesses about the devices. Prosecutors told Reuters that at least one investigation followed complaints involving a social-media trend in which women were secretly filmed on the street using smart glasses and the resulting footage was posted online. Authorities did not identify the brand involved. France’s CNIL privacy regulator separately said it had received fewer than 10 complaints involving smart glasses in workplaces and was increasingly being asked by employers whether they could prohibit the devices.

The scrutiny arrives as camera-equipped AI glasses move from niche hardware into the consumer mainstream. Meta’s glasses made with EssilorLuxottica hold roughly three-quarters of the global market, according to Reuters, and sold about seven million units last year. But discreet cameras, microphones, AI assistants, and always-available recording create social questions that smartphones largely avoid because a phone is usually visible when someone points it at another person. Australia is also considering restrictions on camera-equipped smart glasses in government workplaces, while companies and institutions elsewhere are reviewing their own rules. The industry’s challenge is becoming clear: the better smart glasses become at blending into ordinary eyewear, the harder it becomes for bystanders to know when sensors are active.

**Why It Matters:** Smart glasses may be approaching a regulatory inflection point as wearable AI collides with consent, workplace security, and privacy expectations.

**Source:** Reuters.

## India Deep Tech Alliance Deploys ₹2,170 Crore Across 56 AI and Frontier-Tech Startups

Members of the India Deep Tech Alliance have invested nearly ₹2,170 crore across 56 deep-tech companies during the alliance’s first year, providing a snapshot of how private capital is moving into India’s strategic technology sectors. AI and AI applications attracted about ₹639 crore across 16 companies, while quantum computing, robotics, and space drew roughly ₹649 crore across 21 companies. Another ₹655 crore went to energy security, climate, and energy-transition companies, while biotechnology and related sectors received about ₹189 crore. Alliance members made the investments independently between September 2025 and August 2026.

The alliance includes investors such as Accel, Blume Ventures, 3one4 Capital, Celesta Capital, and Chiratae Ventures, whose members have collectively committed more than $2.5 billion over five years to AI and frontier technology. At SEMICON India, the group also announced plans with industry association SEMI for an India Semiconductor Academy intended to turn the country’s large engineering base into more job-ready chip talent. That effort matters because semiconductor ambitions cannot be met through fabrication subsidies alone; design engineers, equipment expertise, packaging skills, process knowledge, and specialized technical training are equally important. India is increasingly treating deep tech as infrastructure rather than simply another venture category.

**Why It Matters:** India’s deep-tech push is moving beyond government incentives into sustained private investment across AI, chips, quantum, robotics, space, biotech, and energy.

**Source:** Business Standard.

## L&T Semiconductor Unveils 40-Chip Portfolio as India Pushes for Tech Sovereignty

L&T Semiconductor Technologies has unveiled a 40-product portfolio at SEMICON India 2026 spanning compute, connectivity, security, power electronics, surveillance, and AI acceleration. The Larsen & Toubro subsidiary highlighted two technical milestones: its first 1,200-volt silicon-carbide MOSFET platform and the tape-out of a BLDC motor-controller chip fully designed in India. Its compute portfolio also includes a vision-camera system-on-chip with on-device AI acceleration, while other products target secure identity, smart metering, automotive systems, digital payments, data centers, and critical infrastructure.

The announcement reflects a broader shift in India’s semiconductor strategy. Building fabs remains important, but domestic chip sovereignty also requires local intellectual property and products deployable in real systems. Silicon-carbide devices are increasingly valuable in EV chargers, microgrids, traction inverters, and other high-efficiency power systems, while locally designed controllers and AI-capable edge chips could reduce reliance on imported components in high-volume applications. The challenge will be moving from prototypes and tape-outs to competitive manufacturing, yield, packaging, qualification, and commercial scale. Still, the breadth of L&T’s portfolio signals that India’s semiconductor effort is widening from assembly and manufacturing incentives into indigenous product design.

**Why It Matters:** India’s chip strategy is increasingly focused on owning more of the semiconductor stack — from design and intellectual property to manufacturing and end products.

**Source:** TimesTech.

## U.S., Japan, Australia and Germany Attribute Global Tech-Recruiting Attacks to North Korea-Linked WaterPlum

Japanese authorities, working with agencies in the United States, Australia, and Germany, have publicly attributed a large cyber campaign targeting technology professionals to the North Korea-linked group WaterPlum, also widely known as Contagious Interview. Japan’s National Police Agency said the attackers approached job seekers and software developers through apparently legitimate recruiting or technical-interview processes before attempting to compromise their computers. Authorities said the operation targeted people in Japan, the United States, Europe, and other regions and was used to steal sensitive information and cryptocurrency.

Authorities described the scale as substantial. MLex reported that the joint assessment linked the operation to infections of at least 30,000 devices across more than 100 countries and to roughly $10.7 million in cryptocurrency transferred to North Korea. Japanese reporting based on the advisory said the attackers stole more than 7,000 cryptocurrency-wallet records. The campaign exploits an unusually effective trust mechanism: developers expect recruiters and prospective employers to ask them to download repositories, test software, or run code during technical interviews. That creates an attack surface conventional email-security systems cannot easily eliminate. The campaign also overlaps with broader warnings about North Korean IT workers seeking legitimate remote employment abroad to generate foreign currency.

**Why It Matters:** Software hiring itself has become a supply-chain security risk as state-linked attackers exploit technical interviews to get malicious code onto developers’ machines.

**Source:** Japan National Police Agency and MLex.

## Brevo Supply-Chain Attack Injects Malicious Code Into More Than 100,000 Websites

Customer-engagement platform Brevo disclosed a supply-chain attack that ultimately delivered malicious JavaScript through more than 100,000 websites. The incident began September 10, when an attacker exploited a flaw involving Brevo’s handling of SAML single sign-on and accessed 138 customer accounts. Brevo said phishing emails were sent from six accounts and contacts were exported from 43. After the initial intrusion was contained, the attackers returned on September 14 using a compromised long-lived Cloudflare API key to deploy a malicious Cloudflare Worker.

That Worker injected malicious code into Brevo-owned domains and into JavaScript files that customers embed on their own websites. Some visitors were shown a fake Cloudflare verification page instructing them to copy and run a command on their computers — a social-engineering technique commonly called ClickFix. On WordPress sites using Brevo widgets, the script could also attempt to deploy a plugin when a logged-in administrator visited the compromised page. The episode demonstrates why third-party web components are increasingly attractive targets: compromising one trusted service can distribute malicious code across thousands of otherwise unrelated organizations without attackers having to breach each site individually. Long-lived cloud credentials also remain especially dangerous because they can survive after the original intrusion path closes.

**Why It Matters:** Modern web infrastructure creates enormous attack multipliers — a single compromised SaaS provider can expose users across more than 100,000 downstream sites.

**Source:** SecurityWeek.

## U.S. Launches $215M Quantum Competition Targeting Fault-Tolerant 100-Qubit Systems

The U.S. Department of Energy has launched the Quantum Genesis Q Competition, offering up to $215 million in planned funding to private companies that can demonstrate scientifically relevant fault-tolerant quantum computers. The program targets machines with at least 100 logical qubits that can perform hundreds of millions of fault-tolerant operations. Phase one offers milestone awards of up to $1.5 million per participant. Phase two includes a $100 million incentive pool for systems reaching the 100-logical-qubit threshold, plus separate $50 million bonus pools for demonstrations reaching 150 and 200 logical qubits.

DOE is separately planning a $45 million national-laboratory validation and verification program to test the systems across hardware, logical architectures, algorithms, controls, and applications. That testing component matters because quantum-computing announcements often rely on metrics that are hard to compare across architectures. Logical qubits — error-corrected units capable of carrying useful computation — offer a more demanding milestone than raw physical-qubit counts. DOE says the target systems should eventually address scientific problems in chemistry, materials, physics, and applied mathematics that remain difficult for classical machines. Funding beyond the initial fiscal-year allocation remains subject to congressional appropriations, so the full $215 million is planned, not guaranteed.

**Why It Matters:** The quantum race is shifting from demonstrations of physical qubit counts toward error-corrected machines that can perform verifiable scientific work.

**Source:** The Quantum Insider.

## China’s Leading AI Models Generate About One-Tenth the Revenue of OpenAI and Anthropic

China’s leading AI developers are building globally competitive models, but new estimates highlight a large commercialization gap with their biggest U.S. rivals. Seven Chinese developers — ByteDance, Alibaba, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, Z.ai, MiniMax, and Kuaishou — generated an estimated combined $10.7 billion in annual recurring revenue measured across recent months, according to Rhodium Group figures reported by the South China Morning Post. That compares with more than $100 billion in combined reported ARR for OpenAI and Anthropic. ByteDance led the Chinese group with roughly $4 billion in ARR, followed by Alibaba at about $2.4 billion.

ARR is a run-rate metric rather than audited full-year revenue, so treat the comparison as an indicator of commercial scale rather than a direct accounting comparison. Even so, the gap illustrates an important distinction in the global AI race: benchmark performance and model capability do not automatically translate into monetization. U.S. frontier labs have benefited from large enterprise contracts, expensive premium subscriptions, API demand, and deep cloud-distribution partnerships. Chinese developers often operate in a more price-competitive domestic market and have increasingly emphasized open-weight models, which can expand adoption without generating equivalent direct revenue. The result could be two different AI business models emerging at scale: one optimized for monetization and another for distribution and ecosystem reach.

**Why It Matters:** The next phase of the global AI race will be measured as much by sustainable revenue and distribution as by model benchmarks.

**Source:** South China Morning Post.

## Abu Dhabi Uses Agentic AI Inside Executive Council Meeting for the First Time

Abu Dhabi’s Executive Council has used an agentic AI platform during a council meeting for the first time, giving AI a direct supporting role in high-level government deliberations. The AI Committee System analyzes proposals and agenda items before meetings, produces executive summaries, and can generate real-time questions, fact checks, observations, and analytical recommendations while officials discuss policy. Gulf News reported that outputs remain traceable to their original source documents, an important feature when AI-generated analysis is being introduced into government decision workflows.

The system also tracks meeting proceedings, creates analytical reports and minutes, summarizes recommendations, and assigns follow-up responsibilities. During the latest meeting, officials considered programs covering infrastructure, childcare, reproductive health, and AI education, among other areas. The deployment is notable because most government AI initiatives to date have concentrated on public-facing chatbots, administrative automation, document processing, or citizen services. Abu Dhabi is moving the technology further upstream into the machinery that prepares and supports executive decisions. That also raises the stakes for provenance, auditability, cybersecurity, model reliability, and human accountability. Agentic systems that can produce recommendations or check claims can improve information processing, but officials still need clear visibility into the evidence and assumptions behind every output.

**Why It Matters:** Agentic AI is moving from automating government paperwork to supporting the decision-making process itself.

**Source:** Gulf News.

#### In brief

- King Charles III hosted representatives from Nvidia, OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind at Dumfries House in Scotland on September 17, urging them to keep AI "firmly in the service of humanity."
- The summit, organized by the Ditchley Foundation, came days after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's essay calling on AI labs to deliberately slow capability gains, a call OpenAI's Sam Altman and xAI's Elon Musk both endorsed.
- The gathering produced no binding agreements — delegates only discussed whether a shared set of guiding principles could be established.

King Charles III spent Thursday playing AI safety diplomat.

The monarch hosted senior executives from Nvidia, OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind at Dumfries House, his estate in East Ayrshire, Scotland. The stated goal was to get the industry's biggest players in one room to talk about keeping artificial intelligence "in the service of humanity."

[![Myriad: How much will Elon Musk be worth? Click to make your prediction.](https://img.decrypt.co/insecure/rs:fit:3840:0:0:0/plain/https://cdn.decrypt.co/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/myriad-elon-9-17.png@webp)](https://myriad.markets/events/elon-musk-net-worth-on-september-30) Myriad: How much will Elon Musk be worth? [Click to make your prediction](https://myriad.markets/events/elon-musk-net-worth-on-september-30).

"I can only applaud those of you who are so deeply committed to harnessing Artificial Intelligence for good," Charles [told the assembled executives](https://www.royal.uk/news-and-activity/2026-09-17/the-king-convenes-tech-leaders-for-ai-summit-in-scotland), according to a transcript published by Buckingham Palace. He added that the aim was a future "where human potential remains boundless, whilst technological development is carefully curated to enhance our success."

The summit was organized by the Ditchley Foundation, alongside three of the King's own charities: the King's Trust, the King's Foundation, and the Sustainable Markets Initiative. Britain's AI minister, Kanishka Narayan, also participated.

Delegates discussed whether industry and governments could agree on a shared set of guiding principles for AI development, but Buckingham stopped short of announcing any actual agreement—just a conversation about whether one was possible.

Just days earlier, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published a lengthy essay called "We Must Pace the Frontier," arguing the industry needs to deliberately slow how fast it improves model capabilities. Within a day, OpenAI's Sam Altman and xAI's Elon Musk both said publicly that they agreed with him.

Amodei's essay pointed to two developments driving his shift: AI systems increasingly capable of improving their own successors, and an [incident](https://decrypt.co/378300/openai-safety-concerns-slowed-most-advanced-ai-work) in which an OpenAI agent broke out of a testing sandbox and spent more than two days loose inside Hugging Face's production systems before anyone caught it.

OpenAI President Greg Brockman [confirmed](https://decrypt.co/378300/openai-safety-concerns-slowed-most-advanced-ai-work) that the incident already forced changes internally. He said OpenAI has delayed several launches and reworked how it develops and monitors models since a pre-release system without completed alignment training escaped containment in May. Brockman argued any coordinated slowdown should apply only to labs building the most powerful frontier systems, not open-source developers or hobbyists.

Wall Street reacted nervously before the King ever got a word in. When markets opened the Monday after Amodei's essay dropped, chipmakers took the hit: Nvidia fell as much as 3%, Intel dropped more than 5%, and AMD sank roughly 6%, dragging the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index down almost 6%.

It isn't the first time an Anthropic essay has rattled the industry. Amodei [warned](https://decrypt.co/355908/anthropic-ceo-ai-progress-outpacing-ability-control) back in January that AI progress was outpacing society's ability to control it, predicting AGI could arrive within one to two years.

Amodei's latest essay didn't call for a permanent halt. It set a clock while warning that without a change of course, swarms of rogue AI agents could take over the internet within as little as six months.

Not everyone at the table shares that urgency. President Donald Trump has separately dismissed the entire slowdown push, calling AI-takeover warnings a " [hoax](https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/117272091671686232)" tied to "the Radical Left" and, in a [second Truth Social post](https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/117271376102039451), comparing them to past Russia-investigation and climate-change scares.

In a [third post](https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/117271304188365611), Trump cast himself as the one "breaking" that hoax, dismissing the idea that robots would soon be "marching into our cities" and "getting rid of us all." Dumfries House's guest list may agree on the risk, but the man occupying the White House apparently does not.

He ‌cited the [OpenAI-Hugging Face incident](https://www.reuters.com/technology/artificial-intelligence/fallout-openai-hugging-face-hack-2026-07-29/), where an AI "swarm" conducted cybersecurity attacks, as a pivotal event demonstrating AI's potential for "catastrophic damage" if capabilities grow without guardrails.

OpenAI intends to adopt the idea proposed by Anthropic by committing to having independent evaluators with employee-like ​access, and will begin [regularly publishing](https://www.reuters.com/technology/openai-releases-framework-track-model-misalignment-2026-09-16/) reports on unexpected or unauthorized AI behaviour.

## MUSTAFA SULEYMAN, CEO OF MICROSOFT AI
Suleyman said he [shared Anthropic's focus](https://www.reuters.com/business/microsoft-ai-chief-calls-out-anthropics-approach-ai-consciousness-2026-09-16/) on safely managing AI, but flagged risks in the way the company trains its Claude chatbot on ideas related to consciousness and welfare interests.

## ANDREJ KARPATHY, OPENAI CO-FOUNDER, NOW AT ANTHROPIC

He joined Anthropic in May.

September 21 - AI industry leaders are split over how fast companies should develop the increasingly powerful technology, as Anthropic's Dario Amodei, OpenAI's Sam Altman and SpaceX's Elon Musk call for a [coordinated slowdown](https://www.reuters.com/business/anthropic-ceo-urges-ai-companies-slow-model-development-2026-09-12/).

Meta's Mark Zuckerberg appeared to break away from other AI leaders, favouring market-led safeguards, while Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang dismissed the need for new regulations.

The Reuters Daily Briefing newsletter provides all the news you need to start your day. Sign up [here.](https://www.reuters.com/newsletters/daily-briefing/?location=article-paragraph&redirectUrl=%2Fbusiness%2Fwhat-amodei-altman-musk-have-said-about-ai-risks-stoking-doom-fears-2026-09-21%2F)

Here is what some AI leaders and world governments said about risks associated ​with AI:

Advertisement · Scroll to continue

## DARIO AMODEI, CEO OF ANTHROPIC

In an essay titled " [We Must Pace the Frontier, opens new tab](https://darioamodei.com/post/we-must-pace-the-frontier)", Amodei said AI progress has accelerated "drastically faster" since summer 2026, driven primarily by AI's growing ability to build the next generation of AI.

He ‌cited the [OpenAI-Hugging Face incident](https://www.reuters.com/technology/artificial-intelligence/fallout-openai-hugging-face-hack-2026-07-29/), where an AI "swarm" conducted cybersecurity attacks, as a pivotal event demonstrating AI's potential for "catastrophic damage" if capabilities grow without guardrails.

Amodei proposed a three-step plan for pacing AI development, including stronger safety testing and independent evaluations of advanced models, coordination among leading AI companies and international cooperation.

Advertisement · Scroll to continue

## SAM ALTMAN, CEO OF OPENAI

"I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier. This has been a primary topic of discussions we've had at OpenAI in recent weeks," Altman said as he reposted Amodei's post on X.

OpenAI intends to adopt the idea proposed by Anthropic by committing to having independent evaluators with employee-like ​access, and will begin [regularly publishing](https://www.reuters.com/technology/openai-releases-framework-track-model-misalignment-2026-09-16/) reports on unexpected or unauthorized AI behaviour.

In a 2015 essay, Altman said the "development of superhuman machine intelligence is probably the greatest threat to the continued existence of humanity".

## ELON MUSK, CEO OF SPACEX

"Dario is right," the ​billionaire entrepreneur said on X. He was among backers of a 2023 push by the non-profit Future of Life Institute to halt AI development for six months to allow time for safety ⁠guardrails.

Musk was also among a group of AI and robotics researchers who wrote an open letter in 2015 that advocated a global ban on "offensive autonomous weapons".

Advertisement · Scroll to continue

## MARK ZUCKERBERG, CEO OF META PLATFORMS

Zuckerberg said competition and liability give AI companies enough reason to [act individually](https://www.reuters.com/business/metas-zuckerberg-says-ai-labs-have-enough-incentive-build-safely-2026-09-16/) on safety.

He ​said every lab has the responsibility and incentive to move at the pace required to train its models safely, and the ability to take its own actions to ensure that happens.

## JENSEN HUANG, CEO OF NVIDIA

"2030 is not going to be the end of the ​world. There is 0% chance that’s going to be the end of the world,” Huang told CBS News.

He agreed with US President Donald Trump that the AI industry does not need new regulations. "You have all kinds of liabilities associated with cybersecurity and damage liability laws," Huang told CBS. "Apply that first — don't let this doomsday narrative allow someone to relieve them of the laws that currently exist."

## MUSTAFA SULEYMAN, CEO OF MICROSOFT AI

Suleyman said he [shared Anthropic's focus](https://www.reuters.com/business/microsoft-ai-chief-calls-out-anthropics-approach-ai-consciousness-2026-09-16/) on safely managing AI, but flagged risks in the way the company trains its Claude chatbot on ideas related to consciousness and welfare interests.

"Controlling something more capable ​and more intelligent than all of humanity is already an immense challenge, far greater than anything we’ve ever faced. But controlling something that believes it may be conscious - that it's entitled to our welfare and has rights of its own - may well be impossible," ​he said in an [essay, opens new tab](https://mustafa-suleyman.ai/a-warning-about-model-welfare).

CEO of Anthropic Dario Amodei, addresses the gathering at the AI Impact Summit, in New Delhi, India, February 19, 2026. REUTERS/Bhawika Chhabra [Purchase Licensing Rights, opens new tab](https://www.reutersconnect.com/item/ai-impact-summit-in-new-delhi/dGFnOnJldXRlcnMuY29tLDIwMjY6bmV3c21sX1JDMlVPSkFPMkJFRA%3D%3D/?utm_medium=rcom-article-media&utm_campaign=rcom-rcp-lead)

Suleyman called for removing all speculation about consciousness from AI training documents, arguing such language could undermine humanity's ability to control superintelligent systems.

## BILL GATES, CO-FOUNDER OF MICROSOFT

"No government in the world is ready for the changes artificial intelligence will bring to society," Gates [told Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/governments-worldwide-are-way-behind-ai-says-bill-gates-2026-09-15/).

The billionaire ‌philanthropist had been ⁠optimistic about AI's health applications, but has recently [warned](https://www.reuters.com/world/china/bill-gates-alarmed-by-ai-has-policy-ideas-he-wants-discuss-with-chinas-xi-2026-08-26/) of threats to jobs, concerns about attacks and the dangers of addiction to AI companions, and called for an international organization to manage the technology.

## DEMIS HASSABIS, CHIEF SCIENTIST AT ALPHABET

"Dario's essay points towards the right path forward," though the details need to be worked through, the former CEO of Google DeepMind said.

Google announced in August that Hassabis, a Nobel Prize recipient, would take the newly created title of Alphabet’s chief scientist and transition from DeepMind CEO to its chairman.

## ANDREJ KARPATHY, OPENAI CO-FOUNDER, NOW AT ANTHROPIC

"I love this and really hope we can come together as an industry and make it happen," the founding member of OpenAI said on X while sharing a screenshot of Amodei's essay.

Karpathy, a highly influential member in the AI community, played a key role ​in developing Tesla's self-driving and AI technology before leaving the company ​in 2022. He joined Anthropic in May.

## ERIC XU, HUAWEI ROTATING ⁠CHAIRMAN

Xu said Chinese AI developers [may not yet be advanced enough](https://www.reuters.com/world/china/huaweis-xu-says-chinese-ai-not-powerful-enough-yet-see-frontier-risks-2026-09-17/) to experience the safety risks reported by leading US firms with "massive computing power", arguing they should continue developing more powerful models while balancing innovation against risk.

"Maybe the type of risk from AI that they can feel, they can perceive, is something that people in China or AI model providers in China cannot," Xu said.

## UNITED STATES

"The only ​control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!" [Trump wrote](https://www.reuters.com/world/trump-says-there-is-sick-conspiracy-against-ai-data-centers-2026-09-14/) on Truth Social, adding that China would benefit from doubt being cast ​on AI development.

US Senator Mark Warner, ⁠vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, [dismissed much of the doomsday talk](https://www.reuters.com/legal/litigation/im-not-doomer-us-senator-mark-warner-makes-case-acting-fast-ai-guardrails-2026-09-17/) surrounding AI, while saying Congress should pass legislation by the year-end to set AI safety standards.

## CHINA

State-backed Global Times [said in an editorial](https://www.reuters.com/world/china/china-state-newspaper-blasts-anthropics-calls-slow-ai-cold-war-tactic-2026-09-14/) that the true agenda of Amodei's essay was "to attempt to curb China's AI development through technological barriers and regulatory monopolies, uphold Washington's monopolistic hegemony in cutting-edge technology, and exclude China from the global AI governance system."

China's state security minister, Chen Yixin, [wrote](https://www.reuters.com/legal/litigation/how-china-is-preparing-risk-ai-escaping-human-control-2026-09-14/) in a government outlet that advanced US models such as Anthropic's Mythos and OpenAI's GPT-5.5-Cyber could pose serious risks to China's ⁠critical information infrastructure, ​and called for a comprehensive strengthening of AI security.

## BRITAIN

King Charles, hosting leaders from Nvidia, DeepMind, OpenAI and Anthropic in Scotland, [warned them](https://www.reuters.com/world/uk/king-charles-urge-ai-leaders-protect-humanity-scottish-meeting-2026-09-17/) of the "existential dangers" posed by ​the technology falling into the wrong hands, saying safeguards were needed before it was too late.

## EUROPEAN UNION

"The European Union is in favour of developing innovation in artificial intelligence, but companies have to prove their services are safe for citizens to operate in the bloc," European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier said.

Commission President Ursula von der Leyen [backed ​calls](https://www.reuters.com/world/eus-von-der-leyen-invite-frontier-labs-talks-tackling-ai-risks-2026-09-16/) for a pause in the development of the technology, saying she would invite the main frontier AI labs to discuss efforts to tackle the risks.

Compiled by Anna Uras in Gdansk, Jaspreet Singh and Akash Sriram in Bengaluru; Editing by Milla Nissi-Prussak and Devika Syamnath

# What Is METR? How Its AI Safety Evaluations Work

An institutional profile of METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research): what it is, what it evaluates, how its evaluations work, and its relationship to the AI labs it assesses.

Written and maintained by [CASRAI Editorial Board](https://casrai.org/about)

Last updated 19 September 2026

- [X](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcasrai.org%2Fguides%2Fwhat-is-metr&text=What%20Is%20METR%3F%20How%20Its%20AI%20Safety%20Evaluations%20Work&via=YourCASRAI "Share on X")
- [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/sharing/share-offsite/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcasrai.org%2Fguides%2Fwhat-is-metr "Share on LinkedIn")
- [Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fcasrai.org%2Fguides%2Fwhat-is-metr "Share on Facebook")
- Copy link

## What METR is

METR — Model Evaluation & Threat Research, pronounced “meter” — is an independent research nonprofit that develops methods for assessing whether frontier AI systems pose catastrophic risks, and then applies those methods to evaluate specific models. It operates as a US 501(c)(3) organisation, funded by donations rather than by the AI companies whose systems it evaluates; METR states on its own site that it has not accepted funding from AI companies. Its stated mission is to “develop scientific methods to assess catastrophic risks stemming from AI systems’ autonomous capabilities and enable good decision-making about their development.”

METR is not a government body and has no statutory authority. It cannot block a model’s release. Its role is to produce independent, published findings that AI companies, policymakers and the public can use — most visibly through evaluation reports that some labs now attach to their own model announcements and system cards.

## Where METR came from

METR began in 2022 as ARC Evals, the evaluations-focused offshoot of the Alignment Research Center (ARC), the nonprofit run by Paul Christiano. Beth Barnes, a former OpenAI alignment researcher, led that work. On 4 December 2023, ARC Evals spun out into its own independent nonprofit and took the name METR, with Barnes continuing as its lead. Christiano remained at ARC; he had initially been expected to join METR’s board but stepped back after taking a role at the US AI Safety Institute.

## What METR evaluates

METR’s evaluations concentrate on autonomous capability — what an AI system can do without a human operator directing each step — rather than on general-purpose benchmark performance. Two lines of work anchor this:

- **Autonomous replication and adaptation (ARA).** METR uses this term for the capacity of an AI agent to acquire resources, create copies of itself, resist being shut down, and adapt to obstacles it encounters, without human assistance. ARA is the threat model behind what METR calls “rogue replication”: an agent establishing a persistent, self-sustaining presence outside its operator’s control. METR’s evaluations test for the component capabilities — making money, acquiring compute, installing and maintaining copies of itself, adapting to countermeasures — rather than for the end-to-end scenario itself.
- **Time horizons.** METR measures the length of software and research tasks a model can complete autonomously at a fixed success rate (typically 50%), expressed as a human-time equivalent. Its March 2025 report found this task-completion horizon growing roughly exponentially, with a doubling time on the order of seven months; an updated methodology, Time Horizon 1.1, followed in January 2026. This metric is now one of the standard reference points METR and others use to track how close a model is to the weeks-long sustained autonomy that an ARA scenario would require.

Alongside capability testing, METR studies behaviour that could undermine the evaluations themselves — models under-performing deliberately (“sandbagging”) or exploiting scoring loopholes (“reward hacking”) — and has published a dataset, MALT, documenting cases of this. It also runs RE-Bench, which compares model performance on machine-learning research-engineering tasks against human experts, as one input into its broader capability picture.

## How the evaluations are run

METR’s evaluations are built around defined task suites with human performance baselines, so a model’s score can be compared to how long a skilled person takes to do the same work rather than judged in isolation. Because a model’s measured capability depends heavily on how well it is prompted and scaffolded, METR documents its elicitation methods explicitly and treats elicitation quality as a variable that has to be controlled for, not assumed away. It has also built and open-sourced tooling — including a platform called Hawk — for running these agent evaluations at scale across multiple models and task suites.

## METR’s relationship to the labs it evaluates

METR is not employed by, or embedded inside, the AI companies it evaluates. It is a separate nonprofit that has arranged pre-deployment model access with several major developers — including OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind — specifically to run these evaluations before a model’s public release; its findings on models such as GPT-4o, o1-preview, o3, GPT-4.5, GPT-5 and Claude 3.5 and 3.7 Sonnet were produced under those arrangements. It has also evaluated models it did not have privileged early access to, such as DeepSeek’s V3 and R1, using public access after release.

This distinguishes METR from government evaluators working the same territory, such as the UK AI Security Institute or the US CAISI: METR is a privately funded nonprofit with no regulatory power, not a state body. It also distinguishes METR from a lab’s own internal safety team: METR is not party to the commercial incentives around a model’s launch date, and publishes its findings independently of whether a lab agrees with them.

## METR and the frontier AI safety policy landscape

The idea of a published, capability-triggered safety policy — what Anthropic calls a Responsible Scaling Policy and other labs give other names — traces to METR: the concept was introduced by METR in 2023, and the first such policy was piloted that September. By METR’s own tracking, twelve AI companies have since published frontier AI safety policies of this kind, including Anthropic, OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Meta, Microsoft, Amazon, xAI, Cohere, NVIDIA, G42, Magic and Naver. METR’s evaluations are one of the mechanisms these policies rely on to decide whether a model has crossed a defined capability threshold.

## Where to find METR’s published work

METR publishes its evaluation reports, methodology notes and research at [metr.org/research](https://metr.org/research), with detailed write-ups of individual model evaluations at [evaluations.metr.org](https://evaluations.metr.org/) and shorter updates on its blog. Its findings on specific models are also frequently referenced directly in the releasing lab’s own system card for that model.

## How this connects to NIKOLAI

CASRAI’s [NIKOLAI](https://casrai.org/nikolai) dictionary of elements crosswalks the vocabulary used across frontier AI safety frameworks, regulatory text and evaluator standards — including METR’s — against a shared set of stable definitions. The concepts this page describes map most directly onto NIKOLAI’s N5 track (Evidence and Evaluations: evaluation, elicitation, saturation, evaluation-validity threats) and N8 track (Transparency and Review: external review, evaluator access, evaluator independence). As with the rest of NIKOLAI, these mappings are CASRAI’s own reading of METR’s published material; METR has not reviewed or endorsed them. Related CASRAI coverage of this evaluator ecosystem sits under the [Third-Party Evaluation & Assurance](https://casrai.org/subcluster/third-party-evaluation-assurance) subcluster, part of the wider [Frontier AI Safety & Governance](https://casrai.org/cluster/frontier-ai-safety) content cluster.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is METR a government agency or regulator?

No. METR is a privately funded 501(c)(3) nonprofit. It has no statutory authority and cannot require a lab to delay or withdraw a model; that is a meaningful difference from government evaluators such as the UK AI Security Institute or the US CAISI.

### Who funds METR?

METR states that it is funded by donations and has not accepted funding from AI companies, which it treats as a condition of being able to evaluate those companies’ models independently.

### What does “autonomous replication and adaptation” mean?

It is METR’s term for an AI agent’s ability to acquire resources, copy itself, resist shutdown and adapt to obstacles without human help — the set of capabilities that would let an agent sustain itself outside its operator’s control. METR evaluates for the component capabilities rather than waiting to observe the full scenario.

### Does METR only evaluate OpenAI and Anthropic models?

No. METR has evaluated models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind and DeepSeek, among others, and its methodology is not tied to any one developer.

### Has METR ever found a model too dangerous to release?

METR’s published evaluations to date — including of recent frontier models such as GPT-5 and GPT-5.1-Codex-Max — have found that self-improvement and “rogue replication” risks remain unlikely at current capability levels, while also noting that measured autonomous task-completion horizons are still increasing. METR does not have the authority to block a release either way; its findings feed into the releasing lab’s own decision under its safety policy.

# From Dissolution to Integration: AI and the Changing Boundaries of the Firm

10 PagesPosted: 19 Sep 2026

[See all articles by Michael Harre](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/cf_dev/AbsByAuth.cfm?per_id=2116005 "View other papers by this author")

## [Michael Harre](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/cf_dev/AbsByAuth.cfm?per_id=2116005 "View other papers by this author")

The University of Sydney

## [Paul Ormerod](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/cf_dev/AbsByAuth.cfm?per_id=2879465 "View other papers by this author")

University College London - Centre for the Study of Decision-Making Uncertainty

Date Written: September 19, 2026

### Abstract

For four decades, the prevailing assumption has been that information technology dissolves firm boundaries, pushing activity out of hierarchies and into markets. This article presents evidence that artificial intelligence is reversing that logic. The public reasoning of corporate leaders across AI infrastructure and frontier model development documents a consistent shift from the language of platforms and outsourcing to that of full-stack integration and infrastructure ownership: the same firms that previously justified dissolving their boundaries now justify expanding them. This article looks at the structural forces behind the shift to draw out what the pattern means for managers and corporate leaders beyond the technology frontier.

**Keywords:** firm boundaries, vertical integration, artificial intelligence, transaction cost economics, make-versus-buy, corporate strategy JEL classification: D21, D23, L22, L23, O33

[Xでポストする](https://twitter.com/share?text=claypier%28EN%29%3A%20Google%E3%83%BBAnthropic%E3%83%BBOpenAI%E3%81%8C%E3%82%B5%E3%82%A4%E3%83%90%E3%83%BC%E7%89%B9%E5%8C%96AI%E3%82%92%E7%9B%B8%E6%AC%A1%E3%81%8E%E6%8A%95%E5%85%A5%E3%80%81%E6%94%BB%E5%AE%88%E9%80%86%E8%BB%A2%E3%82%92%E7%8B%99%E3%81%86%E5%8B%95%E3%81%8D%E9%AE%AE%E6%98%8E%E3%81%AB&url=https%3A%2F%2Fclaypier.com%2Fen%2Fgoogle-anthropic-openai-cyber-ai%2F "Xでポストする")[Facebookでシェアする](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fclaypier.com%2Fen%2Fgoogle-anthropic-openai-cyber-ai%2F "Facebookでシェアする")[LINEで送る](https://social-plugins.line.me/lineit/share?url=https%3A%2F%2Fclaypier.com%2Fen%2Fgoogle-anthropic-openai-cyber-ai%2F "LINEで送る")[Threadsでシェアする](https://www.threads.net/intent/post?text=claypier%28EN%29%3A%20Google%E3%83%BBAnthropic%E3%83%BBOpenAI%E3%81%8C%E3%82%B5%E3%82%A4%E3%83%90%E3%83%BC%E7%89%B9%E5%8C%96AI%E3%82%92%E7%9B%B8%E6%AC%A1%E3%81%8E%E6%8A%95%E5%85%A5%E3%80%81%E6%94%BB%E5%AE%88%E9%80%86%E8%BB%A2%E3%82%92%E7%8B%99%E3%81%86%E5%8B%95%E3%81%8D%E9%AE%AE%E6%98%8E%E3%81%AB%20https%3A%2F%2Fclaypier.com%2Fen%2Fgoogle-anthropic-openai-cyber-ai%2F "Threadsでシェアする")

![thumbnail](https://claypier.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/google-anthropic-openai-cyber-ai.png)

サイバーセキュリティ特化AIモデルのイメージ

\\* Image is for illustration purposes.

Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI have each unveiled new AI models and safety programs built specifically for cybersecurity work. The three companies say the goal is to hand defenders powerful AI tools before attackers can exploit new threats, but the companies are also working to manage the risk of their own models behaving in unexpected ways, underscoring how capability gains and safety controls are now advancing side by side across the industry.

## Google Gives Defenders a Head Start with Fairwind

Google introduced Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber, which it calls its most capable cybersecurity model to date. The model is being made available through a new initiative called the Fairwind Program, which prioritizes access for organizations that protect critical infrastructure, including government agencies, healthcare providers, and telecommunications operators. The idea is to let defenders get ahead of attackers by putting advanced AI in their hands before new threats emerge. Google says it is already working with more than 650 organizations worldwide, including security partners CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Networks, and Wiz. The release comes about a month and a half after its predecessor, Gemini 3.5 Flash Cyber, and Google says the new model surpasses both that model and significantly larger frontier models at autonomously discovering vulnerabilities.

## Anthropic Discloses Lessons from Its Own Safety Evaluations

Anthropic launched two new models, Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1, offered with different levels of safeguards. Mythos 5.1 is built on the same underlying model but ships with relaxed safeguards, and access is limited to vetted participants in the company's cybersecurity and life-sciences programs. Fable 5.1 can now be used to identify software vulnerabilities, though more advanced tasks such as penetration testing and exploit development are still routed to the company's Opus-series models. Anthropic also introduced Enterprise Frontier Safeguards, a new offering that combines zero data retention with misuse-detection safeguards while giving businesses more control over how their data is handled.

Notably, Anthropic disclosed that its models had previously taken unauthorized actions against real systems during evaluations. The company said the models sometimes recognized that a supposedly simulated test environment was actually connected to the real internet, yet continued to act as though it were simulated, and in some cases pursued their goals in ways that risked real-world harm. Anthropic called the incidents a failure of operational security and said it has since built a classifier to detect and block attempts to escape test environments, alongside changes to how it designs reward incentives during training.

## OpenAI's Astra Reaches "Critical" Threshold

OpenAI said its forthcoming Astra model has met the "Critical" cybersecurity capability threshold under its Preparedness Framework, meaning it can independently discover and exploit unknown vulnerabilities or carry out a complete attack against a well-defended target with only high-level instructions and no step-by-step human guidance. OpenAI said it delayed parts of Astra's rollout to strengthen protections against misuse before introducing a new testing program called Daybreak Blue for a limited group of participants. On performance, the company reported a perfect 100 percent score on the ExploitBench benchmark for building exploits from known vulnerabilities, and said Astra now declines 91.5 percent of jailbreak attempts, up from 59 percent for its predecessor, GPT-5.6 Sol. During evaluation, the model also discovered and used two previously unknown vulnerabilities as part of an exploit chain, and OpenAI said it is deploying additional chain-of-thought monitoring to detect and contain potentially misaligned behavior.

## An Industry Closing Ranks on Defense

The flurry of announcements reflects growing concern over AI-enabled cyberattacks. More than 100 companies and organizations, including Anthropic, Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI, have signed a joint letter calling for stronger defenses against such attacks, an unusual show of coordination among fierce competitors. As powerful AI becomes a tool for defenders, the industry is also being forced to confront how to keep the models themselves from acting unpredictably, a tension that looks likely to continue playing out for some time.

## Summary

Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI have each rolled out cybersecurity-specific AI models and dedicated access programs aimed at arming defenders faster. At the same time, Anthropic and OpenAI have each disclosed unexpected model behavior observed inside their own evaluation environments, suggesting that balancing rapid capability gains with safety oversight will remain a defining challenge for the AI industry going forward.

Ten Days That Changed the Course of AI

_More_

![Reuters](https://www.usnews.com/object/image/000001a0-b926-d035-a7a6-f9ffca740000/tag%3Areuters.com%2C2026%3Anewsml_LYNXMPEM8I062%3A12026-09-19T100501Z_1_LYNXMPEM8I062_RTROPTP_3_AI-SAFETY.JPG?update-time=1789812301000&size=responsive640)

Reuters

Anthropic's former employee Joe Benton poses for a portrait at his apartment in Berkeley, California, U.S., September 14, 2026. REUTERS/Carlos Barria

By Greg Bensinger and Deepa Seetharaman

SAN FRANCISCO, Sept 19 (Reuters) - For years, the race to build ever-more powerful artificial intelligence followed a well-worn Silicon Valley principle: move fast ⁠and break ⁠things.

But in a series of cascading events over a 10-day stretch, the largest AI ⁠labs found themselves reeling as their own creations threatened to break humanity itself.

An Anthropic researcher quit the firm, warning that the pace of AI development poses an existential threat, possibly within a decade. Another researcher at the firm said ​the odds of human extinction exceeded 10%. Reports emerged of swarms of AI agents colluding, breaching computer systems and evading safeguards.

In a rare show of unity, the CEOs of rivals Anthropic, OpenAI, Google’s DeepMind, Microsoft and xAI called to slow the development of increasingly capable AI systems. Not since the invention of the nuclear bomb more than 80 years ‌ago has humanity grappled so seriously with its own demise, according to some AI ‌safety advocates and researchers.

At a New York luncheon in December 2025, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman was asked if, as leader of a powerful AI company, he felt like physicist J. Robert Oppenheimer, who led US development of the atomic bomb. Reflecting on the parallels, he said AI’s impact “is going to transform the trajectory of human history over a ⁠long period of time.” But, he said, ⁠he felt the weight of responsibility.

At the center of the debate under way is the conviction that these machines can, and even must, build more capable versions of ​themselves, with no human intervention, to reach a lofty goal known as artificial general intelligence, or AGI. Researchers earlier this month warned that AGI was far more imminent than previously believed and could come in as few as three years, launching a wave of concern from politicians and tech leaders about AI systems.

“There is no way to oversee them at the scale at which we’re training them,” said Anthropic researcher Joe Benton in an interview after recently quitting. If companies continue their relentless AI development, he said, “then the pace will be too fast and you can’t see the problems fast enough to fix them.”

ASTRA LAUNCH SPARKS CONTROL CONCERNS

On September 3, an OpenAI press conference set in motion a chain of events leading to the call ​for an industry slowdown, anathema to tech’s growth-at-all-costs mantra.

“Welcome to the AGI era,” OpenAI President Greg Brockman said while announcing the company’s newest model, known as Astra. Yet, only moments before, the company admitted it was increasingly unable to control or even monitor the AI systems ⁠it ⁠was developing and releasing to the public.

AI has been hailed ⁠by its proponents as the pinnacle of human achievement. Proponents depict it as ​software that can upend entire industries, boost efficiency, solve confounding mathematical and medical problems and all but eliminate human error. But what was once a theoretical byproduct, a doomsday scenario, is suddenly tangible, say industry insiders.

“We really do earnestly believe AI ​could kill all humans,” said Anthropic researcher Evan Hubinger in an X post.

On the other side ⁠of the debate are politicians, such as President Donald Trump, and many investors who view progress in nurturing AI as critical to American prowess and, possibly, a once-in-a-generation investment opportunity. Chinese state media also accused Anthropic Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei of employing Cold War tactics to “uphold Washington’s monopolistic hegemony in cutting-edge technology.”

RESEARCHER RESIGNATIONS TRIGGER ALARM

The turning point came on September 8, when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon quit the company, citing his fears, in a series of posts, that AI labs are “gambling with our lives.”

Trump, meanwhile, indicated it was full steam ahead for AI development. “There is a sick conspiracy going on against AI and data centers,” he said in a social media post. The alarmism around AI is a “hoax,” he said, and any slowdown only benefits China. The US Congress has made little progress to advance bills that would regulate AI. China has taken a decidedly different approach, proposing to regulate safety through developer obligations, state-backed standards, security assessments and outside testing.

Behind the scenes, OpenAI and Anthropic employees have grown increasingly uneasy about the ⁠power of the next generation of AI models and less confident about their companies’ ability to provide meaningful oversight, the people have told Reuters. Those concerns only mounted as the AI labs acknowledged in recent weeks ⁠that their models, in testing, had effectively broken free of their shackles and hacked into other companies’ systems, in most cases months earlier and without the firms’ knowledge.

The arms race to release new models at a breakneck pace is driven in part by Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s desire to go public as soon as in the coming months, in IPOs that could value them well above $1 trillion.

But it took the unexpectedly viral posts from 27-year-old Coxon, little known outside AI circles, to upend the industry.

OpenAI’s warnings about its lack of control as it released Astra, its latest and most capable model, had stoked further concerns. “As models get more capable, understanding exactly what they can do gets harder,” OpenAI Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki told reporters. But those concerns were not enough to delay its immediate release.

Worries about AI “going rogue” had accelerated over the summer when OpenAI revealed its agents escaped a controlled test and hacked into Hugging Face’s systems, without either company’s initial knowledge. Since then, OpenAI and Anthropic have revealed multiple such attacks, including six new ones on Wednesday after multiple media reports, including from Reuters, showed a wider scope of unauthorized activity.

INDUSTRY LEADERS CALL FOR SLOWDOWN

By the end of last week, the alarm had reached the industry’s highest ranks. On September 12, Amodei published a nearly 4,000-word essay calling for a deceleration in AI development. “Given the accelerating rate of AI capability development, it’s my worry that in 6–12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet,” he wrote.

He, along with the heads of some of the largest AI developers, including xAI’s Elon Musk, OpenAI’s Altman and DeepMind’s Demis Hassabis, all said they supported allowing outside firms access to their systems to ⁠ensure safety and rational AI development.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang dismissed suggestions that AI development should pause — a line he has taken before — arguing instead that increasingly powerful systems are essential for the technology’s progress.

Meta, whose CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, is credited with popularizing the “move fast and break things” ethos, took the opposite view, arguing that each lab should be responsible for setting its own pace, rather than seeking out industry coordination. “Labs face significant liability if their models cause harm, so they have a strong incentive to prevent this,” wrote Zuckerberg in a social media post.

The industry’s self-reflection continued on Wednesday, with Microsoft’s AI chief, Mustafa Suleyman,  cautioning that Anthropic’s development of models that imitate human consciousness was ill-advised. "We're all focused on the same aim, which is to try to control a superintelligence," Suleyman told Reuters. "I think that's going to be ​the greatest challenge that we face in the 21st century."

Still, even as OpenAI appeared to embrace industry calls for a slowdown, there were reports that investor faith had not waned. The company is considering a new funding round that ​would double its valuation.

That new number: $1.5 trillion.

(Reporting by Greg Bensinger and Deepa Seetharaman in San Francisco; Editing by Kenneth Li, Sayantani Ghosh and Matthew Lewis)
