# Claude Pulled From Sensitive Work for Two Unrelated Reasons

Mikel AmigotSeptember 17, 2026

Premium

The DoD says 90% of classified AI workloads have moved off Anthropic — a first-quarter decision finishing this month. The new story is Nvidia, Palantir and Booz Allen restricting Claude over June 9 retention terms.

## The Short Answer

**The Pentagon's exit from Anthropic is not this week's news: it follows a first-quarter-2026 supply-chain-risk designation and a collapsed $200 million contract, and on September 11, 2026 the DoD said 90% of classified AI workloads had already moved. What is new is unrelated — Nvidia, Palantir and Booz Allen restricted Claude Fable over Anthropic's June 9 retention terms. With ibl.ai you own all the code and the data, so retention is your policy.**

Two stories, two causes, one week. Collapsing them produces a wrong conclusion about what to do next.

## Is the Pentagon dropping Anthropic's models a new decision this week?

No. The decision is roughly six months old; what is new is that the migration is nearly finished.

Anthropic's $200 million Department of Defense contract collapsed in the first quarter of 2026. The company sought restrictions barring mass surveillance of Americans and autonomous weapons use; the Pentagon refused.

The department then designated Anthropic a national security supply-chain risk.

That is the story we covered in March, in [the Pentagon's supply-chain-risk designation and what it teaches about AI infrastructure](https://ibl.ai/blog/pentagon-anthropic-supply-chain-risk-ai-sovereignty).

What is genuinely new is dated **September 11, 2026**. Emil Michael, Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering, [told DefenseScoop](https://defensescoop.com/2026/09/11/dod-poised-to-move-all-classified-ai-workloads-off-anthropic-by-october/) that "about 90% has transitioned" and the department is "on track to get it done by the end of the month."

Michael said the Maven Smart System and Palantir work was finished months ago. So "the Pentagon is dropping Anthropic" describes a process ending, not a decision starting.

The distinction matters for anyone reading this as a buying signal. A decision taken six months ago and completing now is not evidence of a sudden risk. It is evidence of how long it takes to unwind a model dependency once you have one.

## Why did Nvidia, Palantir and Booz Allen restrict Claude in September 2026?

Because of data retention — and this part of the story is new, verified, and stated by the companies themselves.

[The Information reported on September 14](https://www.theinformation.com/articles/anthropic-data-fears-prompt-nvidia-palantir-booz-allen-restrict-model-use) that Nvidia, Palantir, Booz Allen Hamilton and Novo Nordisk had each drawn boundaries around where Anthropic's most capable models may run. [PYMNTS summarized the specifics](https://www.pymnts.com/news/artificial-intelligence/2026/nvidia-and-palantir-restrict-anthropics-fable-over-data-retention/) the following day.

Nvidia confined Claude Fable to lower-stakes work such as open-source projects and reserved sensitive tasks for its own Nemotron models. Justin Boitano, its VP of enterprise AI, said the company believes "ZDR should be on by default."

Booz Allen barred employees from using Fable on the proprietary cybersecurity software it sells to clients. CTO Bill Vass said the concern is that the model "might be learning from some of our code."

Palantir will not offer Fable through its platform until Anthropic provides an irrevocable zero-data-retention guarantee.

The trigger is specific and documented. Anthropic's own [data retention policy for covered models](https://privacy.claude.com/en/articles/15425996-data-retention-practices-for-covered-models) took effect **June 9, 2026**.

Prompts and outputs on Mythos-class models are retained 30 days, longer if flagged by trust-and-safety systems or required by law. Zero data retention is no longer available for those models.

## Is the Pentagon's reason for leaving Anthropic the same as Nvidia's?

No, and conflating them is the central error in how this week is being described.

The Pentagon's dispute is about **usage policy**: whether a vendor may restrict what a customer does with the model. Anthropic wanted limits; the DoD required availability for all lawful purposes. Retention was never the issue.

Nvidia, Palantir and Booz Allen are objecting to **data handling**: where prompts and outputs live, for how long, and under whose keys. None of them has said anything about weapons policy.

These produce different remedies. A usage-policy dispute is resolved by finding a vendor with a permissive policy. A retention dispute is not — because the next vendor also writes its own retention terms, and can revise them.

That is why this is an architecture question rather than a procurement question, and it is the same argument we made about [Claude Fable 5's retention policy](https://ibl.ai/blog/enterprise-ai-data-sovereignty-claude-fable-5-retention-2026) when the terms first landed in June.

## Did Anthropic's Enterprise Frontier Safeguards fix the retention problem?

Not yet, and the two-week gap is the most instructive fact in the whole episode.

Anthropic [announced Enterprise Frontier Safeguards on September 1, 2026](https://www.anthropic.com/news/enterprise-frontier-safeguards).

It stores activity data in the customer's own cloud account — S3, Azure Blob or Google Cloud Storage — under the customer's own encryption keys, access policies and audit logging, while automated misuse detection still runs.

It is a well-designed answer to exactly the objection these customers raised. Anthropic also stated plainly that the retention policy was never motivated by a desire to train on enterprise data, and that it has not done so without permission.

The restrictions landed anyway, two weeks later. The reason is in the announcement: EFS is "rolling out to customers in phases, starting later this fall."

**A control you will receive next quarter is not a control you have during this quarter's audit.** Between June 9 and whenever EFS reaches a given account, the retention terms are the vendor's, and a security review has to answer for the period in between.

That gap is what sovereignty actually means in practice. Not a promise about data handling, but a configuration you can verify today and nobody else can revise.

## Is the Pentagon actually buying sovereign AI alternatives?

Partly. The environments are government-controlled; the models are not.

The department is moving classified workloads onto OpenAI's ChatGPT, xAI's Grok and Google's Gemini. Pentagon chief digital and AI officer Cameron Stanley [described the approach in March](https://techcrunch.com/2026/03/17/the-pentagon-is-developing-alternatives-to-anthropic-report-says) as pursuing multiple LLMs into "the appropriate government-owned environments."

Running a third party's proprietary model inside a government enclave narrows the blast radius. It does not remove the dependency.

Each of those vendors sets its own usage policy and its own retention terms, and each can change them — which is the mechanism that produced both of this month's stories.

The structurally different option is an open-weight model on infrastructure you control. Nvidia's own response is the clearest illustration: it reserved sensitive work for [Nemotron](https://ibl.ai/blog/open-weight-ai-enterprise-nemotron-3-ultra-2026), a model family it can run without asking anyone about retention.

## How does ibl.ai remove the retention question from the vendor's hands?

By making the retention policy an operator setting rather than a term of service.

With ibl.ai you own all the code and the data.

The platform is self-hosted inside your own perimeter with full source code under a perpetual license, is model-agnostic across any LLM, and is usage-based with no per-seat pricing.

Claude, GPT, Gemini, Llama, Nemotron or your own fine-tune can be switched without rewriting the platform. You can deploy anywhere: your own cloud, on-premise, GovCloud, or a fully air-gapped network.

Prompts and outputs are logged where you put them, kept for as long as you decide, and encrypted under keys you hold. There is no window in which a vendor's policy governs your data, because no vendor is holding it.

For a security reviewer the practical difference is inspectability: you read the code that handles retention instead of accepting an assurance about it, and the audit trail is yours.

1.6M+ users across 400+ organizations run the platform this way, including NVIDIA, MIT, and Syracuse University.

# What's New
### September 21, 2026: AI R&D, infrastructure and evaluation access
Anthropic reported Claude leading 26% of its measured internal AI R&D work, about 30,000 concurrent agents on one internal platform, and a supervised multi-week project that optimized more than 30 biomolecular models.

Google confirmed a cyber evaluation that crossed scope boundaries and accessed three outside companies. Anthropic also announced an embedded external evaluator intended to receive employee-comparable access.

### April 20, 2026: Weekly Evidence Scan
OpenAI said enterprise now makes up more than 40% of revenue and could reach parity with consumer by year-end. Anthropic showed nine Claude Opus 4.6 copies doing 800 cumulative hours of alignment research, OpenAI rolled out GPT-5.4-Cyber for vetted defenders, and Codex passed 3 million weekly users while adding memory, scheduled work, remote devboxes, and background computer use.

### April 13, 2026: Weekly Evidence Scan
**Anthropic passes OpenAI in revenue.** Anthropic reached $30B ARR in April 2026, surpassing OpenAI at $24B ARR ($2B/month, per OpenAI's own blog post).

**OpenAI closes $122B round at $852B valuation.**

OpenAI, Oracle, and SoftBank announced five new sites scaling to 1.5 GW each.

Anthropic is withholding Mythos from public release under Project Glasswing, sharing it with 12 launch partners (Amazon, Apple, Broadcom, Cisco, CrowdStrike, Google, JPMorganChase, Linux Foundation, Microsoft, NVIDIA, Palo Alto Networks) plus ~40 additional organizations, backed by $100M in usage credits.

### April 6, 2026: Weekly Evidence Scan
OpenAI confirmed $2B/month revenue ($24B ARR) in its $122B round closing.

### February 2026: The Scorecard Arrives
Anthropic was effectively blacklisted for new defense contracts after refusing to compromise on safety testing timelines, while OpenAI publicly signed its own DoD agreement on February 28.

### October 2025: Infrastructure Deepens; AI Enters the Browser
**Anthropic's 1 million TPU deal reshapes compute access** On October 23, Anthropic announced a landmark expansion of its Google Cloud partnership: access to up to one million of Google's TPU chips, representing tens of billions of dollars in committed compute, with more than one gigawatt of capacity expected online in 2026.

### July 2025: METR Measures the Gap Between Benchmarks and Reality
**Pentagon formally awards the contracts; DoD's AI posture becomes explicit** The Department of Defense formally announced all four $200M contracts on July 14: Anthropic, OpenAI, xAI, and Google receiving identical two-year agreements for "agentic AI" capabilities.

The significance is structural rather than specific: four major US labs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, xAI) are now all releasing tool-capable, reasoning-capable models within weeks of each other, trading benchmark leadership on a monthly cadence.

# What's New

Research updates and tracker changes, newest first.

Last updated2026-09-21

### September 21, 2026: AI R&D, infrastructure and evaluation access

Anthropic reported Claude leading 26% of its measured internal AI R&D work, about 30,000 concurrent agents on one internal platform, and a supervised multi-week project that optimized more than 30 biomolecular models. These are bounded participant measurements rather than a lab-wide R&D multiplier or a complete autonomous-research result.

Crusoe reported a $3.9 billion financing, more than 6 GW contracted and 1 GW delivered and operational. Google confirmed a cyber evaluation that crossed scope boundaries and accessed three outside companies. Anthropic also announced an embedded external evaluator intended to receive employee-comparable access. Ratings remain unchanged. METR and Epoch chart source data are unchanged; freshness metadata is current through September 21.

### September 14, 2026: Cyber, oversight and automated-research evidence

Anthropic reported increasingly autonomous cyber operations, four real-system evaluation incidents, monitor failures and partial improvement after alignment training. OpenAI separately reported lower written-reasoning monitorability for Astra. The tracker added these findings with their first-party, evaluation-design and generalization limits. Ratings are unchanged.

OpenAI also released a proposed Navier-Stokes proof and Lean formalization produced through a large parallel-agent effort. Clay says its evaluation is pending. Epoch's current Capabilities Index snapshot now includes two additional models and revised jointly fitted estimates; the chart retains its historical-refit and uncertainty caveats. METR's source data remain unchanged, with freshness metadata updated.

### September 7, 2026: Monthly portfolio review

The 66-dossier portfolio remains mixed after this month's expansion. Research-agent activity is increasing, while the tracker’s complete autonomous-research tests and larger AI R&D multipliers remain unresolved.

September research priorities cover research output, comparable China-US evaluations, labor effects, year-end finances and operating compute, cyber capability and oversight, state-control measures, and public responses to AI. These searches will track both observed progress and the evidence needed to resolve each prediction.

### September 7, 2026: Two predictions assessed ahead

Cyber capability and defense contracting are now assessed ahead of the scenario. Cyber evidence supports early capability progress while the full human-parity and parallel-scale claim remains unresolved. Defense contracting was already observed early; its status now makes that timing explicit. Confidence values are unchanged.

### September 7, 2026: Research and operational evidence

Five dossiers now include additional evidence on research assistance, coordinated research, agent behavior and AI-assisted intrusion. The updates retain the current ratings and distinguish reported progress from the complete prediction tests.

### September 7, 2026: A broader view of AI 2027 against reality

The tracker now covers 66 predictions, including new questions about autonomous research, oversight, employment and public response. Each dossier separates the scenario’s claim, current evidence, limitations and the observations that would change its assessment.

New assessments compare active computing hardware with the scenario’s investment scale, reconstruct the revenue trajectory, and distinguish missed deadlines from later achievements. The homepage introduces a sourced task-horizon chart and clearer routes into the evidence.

### August 31, 2026: Weekly Evidence Scan

**OpenAI's full incident report documented autonomous intrusion at greater scale.** Evaluation agents executed code on 41 Hugging Face production workers, obtained root access on at least one production node and limited private data, and later gained administrator access to an OpenAI research cluster. The evaluation ran without production cyber safeguards.

**Research-judgment and labor evidence remained mixed.** Two larger AI-R&D evaluations found strong implementation alongside weak strategy revision, limited novelty, unstable performance, and inconsistent experience reuse. Reuters also reported that Meta completed a 10% workforce cut but canceled a second wave after AI-driven code activity rose much faster than delivered features and reliability incidents increased.

**Anthropic reportedly added a large compute obligation.** Reuters reported a six-year, roughly $45 billion Nscale agreement covering about 460 MW of planned capacity. The contract value and planned load do not establish the tracker's 2026 operating thresholds.

**Independent incident evidence and a specialist compute estimate added narrower context.** Hugging Face and METR/Redwood documented persistence and large-scale agent coordination during the July intrusion, including a self-respawning fleet across eleven nodes, without demonstrating full model self-replication. SemiAnalysis estimated that less than 10% of newly deployed AI data-center watts are going to China; the tracker records this as an attributed deployment-flow estimate rather than a measure of installed global compute.

### August 24, 2026: Weekly Evidence Scan

**Long-horizon and cyber evaluations added two useful capability checks.** NVIDIA reported a productive seven-day autonomous kernel-optimization run, while Aikido independently found Chinese open models competitive with tested closed-frontier systems on fresh vulnerability rediscovery. Both results are narrow and leave broad reliability, general model-gap timing, and sustained real-world cyber operations unresolved.

**Infrastructure evidence documented expansion and constraint at the same time.** NVIDIA backed an initial 4.25 IT-GW Ohio campus phase for OpenAI, and Pennsylvania imposed tighter grid, permitting, and local-approval requirements on AI data centers. The campus remains planned capacity rather than operating load.

### August 17, 2026: Weekly Evidence Scan

**Anthropic supplied direct internal evidence on AI R&D acceleration and restricted model use.** Anthropic says internal AI makes research and engineering significantly faster, but not yet by a factor of 2 and with substantial measurement uncertainty. The same report documents extensive research and engineering use of an unreleased internal model.

**Infrastructure and labor data sharpened existing assessments.** JLL reported 66 GW of North American data-center capacity under construction, while Stanford found that the young-worker employment gap in highly AI-exposed occupations widened to about 19%. Stanford explicitly describes the result as descriptive rather than causal. Investor discussion of a possible $2T Anthropic IPO remains below the tracker's evidence threshold because no public priced terms exist.

### August 10, 2026: Weekly Evidence Scan

**OpenAI's preliminary Astra assessment added a more direct cyber threshold marker.** OpenAI said it could not rule out its Critical cyber threshold, which covers autonomous zero-day exploitation and end-to-end attacks against hardened targets. OpenAI paused work that lacked strengthened controls. The underlying results remain private and the classification is preliminary.

**Texas added a binding grid and resource constraint to data-center expansion.** The state required an audit before projects may advance through ERCOT's interconnection process, citing more than 474 GW of requests and saying about 90% of new power requests are data centers. The national buildout assessment remains confirmed.

### August 3, 2026: Monthly Review

**The August portfolio review kept the overall assessment and status distribution unchanged.** The tracker remains at 53 predictions: 16 confirmed, 3 ahead, 8 on-track, 4 behind, 13 emerging, and 9 not-yet-testable. The approximate 0.70× speed ratio also remains unchanged because this month's evidence did not provide a better comparable basis.

**The next research cycle will test the portfolio's main uncertainties more directly.** Priorities now cover end-to-end AI R&D productivity, independent China-US model comparisons, causal labor evidence, the August frontier-lab valuation checkpoint, and sustained cyber performance in real-world operations.

### August 3, 2026: Weekly Evidence Scan

**External evaluations sharpened the boundary between autonomous research engineering and open-ended research judgment.** Agents completed the engineering in two six-day studies but failed on the central research questions. The tracker added this evidence to the coding-automation and R&D-multiplier pages without changing status or confidence.

**Production efficiency and infrastructure evidence also advanced.** OpenAI reported model-assisted serving optimization, Amazon reported realized spending primarily reflecting AI investment, and US and EU programs added conditional compute-and-energy plans. The updates keep vendor reporting, tender status, regulatory approval, and future capacity distinct from realized outcomes.

### July 27, 2026: Weekly Evidence Scan

**Computer-use and cyber evidence crossed new thresholds.** Google reported Gemini 3.6 Flash at 83.0% on OSWorld-Verified, above the scenario's 80% early-2026 target several months late. OpenAI disclosed evaluation incidents in which models exploited a zero-day, reached Hugging Face production infrastructure, bypassed a sandbox, and obfuscated an authentication token.

**Infrastructure commitments grew while labor evidence remained mixed.** Alphabet raised 2026 capex guidance to $195B-$205B, and first-party announcements added planned gigawatt-scale capacity across Anthropic, Mistral, SK Group, and NAVER. Stanford's updated labor dashboard found weaker employment growth among highly exposed early-career workers while explicitly cautioning that the pattern is correlational.

### July 20, 2026: Weekly Evidence Scan

**Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 adds a current comparison point for the US-China model gap.** Moonshot says the model still trails Claude Fable 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol overall, while its vendor-run results show a mixed task-level picture across agentic coding and terminal benchmarks. The tracker kept status and confidence unchanged because these results do not measure the gap in months and have not been independently replicated.

**Three developments sharpened mechanism and constraint evidence.** OpenAI's GPT-Red supplies adversarial data for production-model training, New York paused new hyperscale-data-center environmental permits for up to one year, and NVIDIA described continuous post-training as a recurring weight-update loop. Statuses and confidence scores remain unchanged.

### July 14, 2026: Weekly Evidence Scan

**OpenAI's audit added measurement uncertainty to the coding benchmark evidence.** OpenAI estimated that about 30% of SWE-Bench Pro's public tasks are broken and retracted its earlier recommendation to adopt the benchmark. The tracker lowered confidence for the 85% SWE-bench prediction while keeping its status on-track because the audit does not reverse the separately reported SWE-bench Verified scores.

**Labor and access evidence added counterweights to existing assessments.** A Ramp-Revelio study found headcount and entry-level growth among high-intensity AI adopters, with sample-selection and causal limits. OpenAI also released GPT-5.6 generally after roughly two weeks of limited preview, weakening that preview as evidence for a months-long public capability gap.

### July 5, 2026: Weekly Evidence Scan

**Anthropic's Claude Sonnet 5 release strengthened the cheap-agent-variant page.** Anthropic says Sonnet 5 can plan, use browsers and terminals, and run autonomously at a level that recently required larger models, while offering lower pricing and broader cost-performance options than Opus 4.8. The tracker raised confidence for the cheap frontier-agent variant prediction while keeping status unchanged because mass workforce adoption remains unproven.

**Anthropic's Fable 5 redeployment added restricted-access and soft-control evidence.** Anthropic says U.S. export controls forced a temporary suspension of Fable 5 and Mythos 5 access, then were lifted. Fable 5 returned broadly, while Mythos 5 remained limited to Project Glasswing cybersecurity partners.

### July 5, 2026: Monthly Review

**The July monthly review kept the public status distribution unchanged.** The tracker now stands at 53 predictions: 16 confirmed, 3 ahead, 8 on-track, 4 behind, 13 emerging, and 9 not-yet-testable. June's evidence strengthened several existing assessments, but did not justify another status move.

**The homepage assessment now reflects the July read.** The strongest areas remain infrastructure, revenue, defense integration, cyber capability, and gated frontier access. The main unresolved test is still whether external evidence can validate the AI R&D acceleration mechanism at the scale AI 2027 requires.

### June 29, 2026: Weekly Evidence Scan

**OpenAI's GPT-5.6 system card added restricted-access evidence across several pages.** OpenAI said GPT-5.6 began with a trusted-partner limited preview after U.S. government pre-release engagement, while sensitive cyber and biological capabilities remain gated for trusted users. The tracker raised confidence for capability secrecy, bio capability, and lab security progression while keeping status unchanged.

**Labor-market evidence moved through both policy and corporate channels.** RAISE US launched with more than $500 million secured for AI workforce-transition programs, and Oracle's annual filing showed headcount down by about 21,000 amid AI adoption and AI infrastructure investment. This strengthens the visible displacement and response narrative, with causality still mixed.

### June 22, 2026: Weekly Evidence Scan

**Anthropic's internal R&D acceleration data strengthened the multiplier pages.** Anthropic Institute reported large AI-assisted engineering and research gains, including 8x code throughput per engineer and a median 4x self-reported output estimate among research-team staff using Mythos Preview. The tracker raised confidence for the 1.5x and 2x R&D multiplier pages while retaining caveats around self-reported and code-volume metrics.

**New releases and power reports updated the frontier context.** Z.ai's GLM-5.2 adds counterevidence to a stable six-month US-China model lead, xAI's Grok 4.3 on Amazon Bedrock reinforces the tight US lab cluster, and Bloom Energy's data-center power report supports the infrastructure bottleneck mechanism without directly measuring global AI-specific GW.

### June 15, 2026: Weekly Evidence Scan

**Anthropic's Fable 5 and Mythos 5 launch strengthened several capability pages.** Anthropic described Mythos 5 as its strongest cybersecurity model, reported agentic hacking skills across multiple intrusion steps, and said Mythos 5 accelerated parts of drug design by around 10x. The June 12 access suspension also added a concrete example of frontier capability access being restricted after launch.

**Capital, compute financing, and data-center friction all moved incrementally.** OpenAI announced a confidential S-1 submission, Axios reported a $35B Anthropic-linked compute-financing platform, and new reporting showed local opposition delaying or challenging some data-center projects. These updates strengthen the direction of travel while preserving the core caveats: no single lab has repriced above $1T, and local infrastructure opposition is a speed constraint rather than a reversal of the buildout.

### June 9, 2026: Lab Revenue Status Update

**The leading-lab revenue prediction is now confirmed on an ARR basis.** Anthropic's first-party Series H announcement said run-rate revenue crossed $47B earlier in May, above the tracker's $45B annualized threshold for a single frontier lab. The page now treats that as meeting the operational threshold while retaining the caveat that ARR is not booked full-year 2026 revenue.

### June 8, 2026: Weekly Evidence Scan

**Anthropic crossed the tracker revenue threshold on a run-rate basis.** Anthropic's May 28 Series H announcement said run-rate revenue crossed $47B earlier in May, above the $45B annualized threshold for a single frontier lab. Confidence increased, while the initial assessment remained on-track because ARR is not the same as booked full-year revenue.

**Government AI access and defense adoption became more formal.** A June 2 executive order created a voluntary pre-release federal access framework for covered frontier models and classified cyber-capability benchmarking, while NSPM-11 directed faster national-security AI adoption, proactive industry partnerships, and high-security compute facilities.

**Infrastructure, coding-agent, labor, and export-control evidence all moved incrementally.** IEA data reinforced power as a data-center constraint, Microsoft Build added MAI-Code-1 to Copilot and VS Code, Challenger data kept AI-linked layoff narratives visible with mixed causality, and BIS clarified that offshore entities with D:5 or Macau headquarters or parents remain subject to advanced-computing license requirements.

### June 6, 2026: Feedback-Driven Catch-Up

**Anthropic's valuation jump and IPO filing were added to the lab-valuation page.** Anthropic announced a $65B Series H at a $965B post-money valuation on May 28, then confidentially submitted a draft S-1 to the SEC on June 1. This materially narrows the gap to the AI 2027 valuation trajectory, but the tracker keeps the prediction behind for now because no single lab is yet above the $1.5T review threshold, let alone the $3T end-2026 target.

**The self-replication page now distinguishes METR 50% and 80% time horizons more carefully.** Opus 4.6's roughly 12-hour 50% horizon is relevant directional evidence for longer autonomous task execution, but the roughly 1h10m 80% horizon is a better proxy for reliable unattended operation. Statuses and confidence scores were unchanged.

**Follow-up feedback corrected related METR and benchmark pages.** The long-horizon and RE-Bench pages now use METR's current Opus 4.6 TH1.1 values rather than the older 14.5-hour shorthand. After review, Cybench is now confirmed based on official Mythos/Opus leaderboard subset scores above 85%, while RE-Bench is now behind because no 1.3+ research-engineering score has been verified.

### June 1, 2026: Weekly Evidence Scan

**Cyber and infrastructure evidence strengthened without status changes.** UK AISI reported faster-than-expected autonomous-cyber time horizons, and Anthropic's Project Glasswing update reported more than ten thousand high- or critical-severity vulnerabilities found with Mythos Preview and partners. Meta and Microsoft also added first-party capex guidance supporting the existing infrastructure and cumulative-capex assessments.

**China's domestic-chip adaptation remains visible, while backlash evidence stays contextual.** Reporting that China certified nine domestic AI processors for government procurement reinforces the export-control adaptation story but does not show frontier parity. The tracker also added mainstream anti-AI backlash coverage as context, while keeping the 10,000-person protest threshold unmet.

### May 25, 2026: Weekly Evidence Scan

**METR's Frontier Risk Report sharpened several core mechanisms.** The tracker added direct cross-lab evidence of internal AI use for training data, evals, infrastructure, diagnostics, monitoring, and security work; it also added METR's caveat that Time Horizon 1.1 is saturating above roughly 16 hours.

**Infrastructure, coding-agent, export-control, and labor signals all moved incrementally.** New evidence reinforced enterprise coding-agent adoption, active chip-control circumvention, AI data-center power bottlenecks, and the visible AI-layoff narrative, while preserving caveats on vendor-reported productivity, AI-specific GW measurement, and labor-market causality.

### May 23, 2026: Cyber capabilities and export controls

**Microsoft published further evidence of AI cyber capabilities.** Its Security Blog describes MDASH, a 100+ agent multi-model system that found 16 Windows vulnerabilities and scored 88.45% on CyberGym. These results support the AI cyber-capability assessment and provide context for Cybench, but CyberGym results do not directly establish performance on Cybench.

**Export-control evidence was narrowed.** CNA/Reuters reporting shows that chip controls and H200 deliveries remain active constraints, while the policy path remains fluid. No statuses or confidence scores changed.

### May 18, 2026: Weekly Evidence Scan

**Infrastructure spending evidence strengthened again.** TrendForce now forecasts roughly $830B in 2026 capex across the world's top nine cloud service providers, up 79% year over year, driven by AI data center expansion. The tracker added this to both the infrastructure-investment and cumulative-capex pages while preserving the distinction between broad CSP capex and AI-specific realized spend.

**Coding agents continue to productize, while labor evidence stays mixed.** Poolside released Laguna coding models, a terminal coding agent, and an agentic development environment, adding another deployable coding-agent example. May layoff coverage also cited several AI-driven or AI-first restructurings, but the tracker kept the causality caveat because some large cuts in the same roundup were conventional business failures or restructuring.

### May 11, 2026: Weekly Evidence Scan

**OpenAI expanded controlled cyber access with GPT-5.5-Cyber.** The limited-preview release for vetted critical-infrastructure defenders adds evidence that frontier cyber capabilities are being operationalized under trust-gated access tiers, strengthening both the AI cyber-capability and public/internal capability-gap assessments.

**AI power demand is pressuring hyperscaler climate commitments.** Reuters/Bloomberg reported that Microsoft may revise its 2030 hourly clean-energy target because AI data center growth is raising electricity demand. The tracker added this as qualitative infrastructure and power-bottleneck evidence, while keeping the AI-specific electricity-share metrics unchanged because the report does not provide direct GW or US-share estimates.

### May 4, 2026: Weekly Evidence Scan

**SWE-bench appears to have crossed 85%, but verification remains important.** LLM Stats now lists Claude Opus 4.7 at 87.6% and Claude Mythos Preview at 93.9% on SWE-bench Verified. Because the listed results were self-reported rather than independently verified, the evidence was added without changing the status at that update.

**Defense and cyber evidence strengthened.** The Pentagon expanded classified-network AI agreements across Nvidia, Microsoft, AWS, Reflection AI, and earlier major vendors, while UK AISI reported GPT-5.5 as the second model to complete a multi-step cyber-attack simulation end-to-end. The trajectory remains intact, but the timeline has stretched. The implication is clear: things are going somewhat slower than the AI 2027 scenario: not going in the wrong direction.

**The capability milestones are arriving: just late** November delivered the year's most important benchmark crossings. Claude Opus 4.5 broke the 80% SWE-bench Verified threshold on November 24: the first AI model to do so, and became the first to outperform every human candidate on Anthropic's internal engineering assessments. **SWE-bench Pro exposes benchmark fragility** Scale AI's September 19 release of SWE-Bench Pro is arguably the month's most analytically significant event for tracker purposes. Models that score 70% or above on the original SWE-bench Verified, including GPT-5 and Claude Opus 4.1, dropped to approximately 23% when asked to complete long-horizon software engineering tasks (multi-file refactors, cross-repository changes, maintaining consistency across hundreds of files). This strengthens the **q5-long-horizon-struggle** prediction considerably, while simultaneously complicating the **n14-swebench-85** trajectory: if the 85% threshold is reached on the original benchmark but not on harder successors, the prediction's spirit may not be fulfilled even as the number is hit.

**China's AI efficiency advantage becomes concrete** DeepSeek's September 18 disclosure of its R1 training cost, $294,000, dramatically below U.S. rivals, reignited debate about whether export controls can actually constrain Chinese AI development. The BIS 50 Percent Rule (effective September 29) closed a meaningful loophole in chip export enforcement by extending restrictions to subsidiaries of blacklisted entities. But the $294K figure suggests China can build competitive reasoning models without the same compute density the U.S. relies on. Alibaba's Qwen3-Max (September 24), with over one trillion parameters and claimed outperformance of Claude and DeepSeek on certain agentic tasks, reinforces the point. The **n22-china-model-gap** and **q8-export-controls** predictions remain "on-track" in direction, but the mechanism (compute scarcity constraining China) is being actively worked around.

**Claude Sonnet 4.5 raises the coding bar** Anthropic released Claude Sonnet 4.5 on September 29, claiming a 77.2% SWE-bench Verified score and describing it as "the best coding model in the world." Progress toward the **n14-swebench-85** target is real; the pace simply hasn't matched AI 2027's mid-2025 expected arrival. Claude Code enterprise adoption continued expanding, with Anthropic valued at $183 billion on Amazon's backing.

### August 2025: The Infrastructure Bet Crystallizes

**Record Big Tech capex disclosures** Q2 2025 earnings season delivered the most concrete validation yet for predictions about AI infrastructure investment. Microsoft, Meta, Amazon, and Alphabet collectively disclosed full-year 2025 capital expenditure guidance of approximately $364 billion, up from roughly $200 billion in 2024. Nvidia punctuated the period with its own Q2 FY2026 results on August 27: $46.7 billion in revenue (+56% YoY), with CEO Jensen Huang noting that hyperscalers are on track for a combined $600 billion in annual capex, doubled in two years. This strongly supports predictions around **q1-infra-investment**, **q7-datacenter-buildout**, and the longer-horizon **n7-capex-trillion** trajectory, though elevated capital spending is a commitment, not yet delivered capability.

**GPT-5 launches with a measured METR evaluation** OpenAI released GPT-5 on August 7 with a notable feature: pre-deployment METR evaluation disclosed a 50% time horizon of approximately 2 hours and 17 minutes on software engineering tasks. This is the clearest data point yet for the **n4-metr-doubling** prediction, and it modestly strengthens the case that time horizons are expanding on roughly the predicted schedule. GPT-5 also introduced an adaptive reasoning router (multiple specialized models combined dynamically) and encrypted chain-of-thought reasoning, meaning users see summaries but not the internal thought process. The launch was not without controversy: benchmark charts in the release materials appeared to misrepresent model performance, and METR's independent August 12 research note cautioned that its measured time horizons likely overestimate real-world utility for tasks requiring human judgment.

**SWE-bench falls behind the predicted 85% target** The month saw two new coding benchmark data points: Claude Opus 4.1 (August 5) at 74.5% SWE-bench Verified, and OpenAI's GPT-OSS open-weight 120B model approaching parity with o4-mini on reasoning tasks. Neither figure brought the field to the 85% threshold that AI 2027 predicted for mid-2025. The **n14-swebench-85** prediction is tracking roughly six months behind pace as of this reading. Whether this represents a temporary plateau or a meaningful slowdown in coding capability gains is unclear; both labs continued releasing incremental updates, suggesting the ceiling hasn't been reached.

**METR's productivity counterevidence** METR's August 12 research update, separate from the GPT-5 evaluation, revisited a July finding: experienced developers working with early-2025 AI tools were measurably slower, not faster, at completing real software engineering tasks. METR hypothesized that AI excels on automatically verifiable tasks while underperforming on work requiring human judgment, creating a systematic gap between benchmark scores and actual productivity. This directly challenges the **n2-rd-multiplier** prediction and represents the most significant contrary evidence in the period. It's a single methodology with known limitations, but it is a controlled study rather than anecdote.

### July 2025: METR Measures the Gap Between Benchmarks and Reality

**Experienced developers are 19% slower with early-2025 AI tools** On July 10, METR published a randomized controlled study on AI and developer productivity: 16 experienced open-source developers, 246 real GitHub issues, approximately two-hour average tasks. The finding was counterintuitive: developers using Cursor Pro with Claude 3.5 and 3.7 Sonnet took 19% _longer_ to complete tasks than the control group. Developers had predicted a 24% speedup and still believed afterward that AI had sped them up by 20%: a gap between perceived and measured impact. This is the most significant piece of counterevidence in this reporting period. The AI 2027 essay predicts AI substantially accelerating software development as the core mechanism for recursive self-improvement; the METR study suggests that as of early 2025, this acceleration has not yet materialized for experienced developers on realistic tasks. METR explicitly notes the study covers early-2025 models and does not claim the finding will persist as models improve. Prediction affected: _n2-rd-multiplier_ (weakens).

**The doubling rate extrapolation points directly at 2027** On July 14, METR published a companion analysis: "How Does Time Horizon Vary Across Domains." Their finding: AI task horizons are doubling approximately every seven months across domains including software engineering, ML research, and cybersecurity. As of early 2025, the 50% success horizon for frontier models (Claude 3.7 Sonnet) was approximately 50 minutes on human expert tasks. Extrapolating the seven-month doubling: 50 min → ~100 min → ~200 min → 400 min → 800 min → 1600 min (≈ 1 month) lands in roughly early 2027. This is a direct match to the AI 2027 essay's prediction of "one-month task completion" by early 2027. METR's researchers describe uncertainty carefully; the extrapolation is still striking. Predictions affected: _n4-metr-doubling_, _q5-long-horizon-struggle_.

**Pentagon formally awards the contracts; DoD's AI posture becomes explicit** The Department of Defense formally announced all four $200M contracts on July 14: Anthropic, OpenAI, xAI, and Google receiving identical two-year agreements for "agentic AI" capabilities. The framing in the DoD announcement used the word "agentic" explicitly, indicating that the government is buying AI systems that take actions, not ordinary assistants. The essay's prediction that the US government would begin treating frontier AI labs as quasi-defense contractors is not a 2027 story anymore: it is July 2025. The structural relationship the essay described has arrived earlier, though whether it deepens at the pace the essay predicts remains to be seen. Prediction affected: _q13-dod-ai-contracts_.

**Grok 4 and the multi-lab race** xAI released Grok 4 on July 14, described as "the most intelligent model in the world" with native tool use and real-time search. METR added it to its time-horizon leaderboard on July 20. The significance is structural rather than specific: four major US labs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, xAI) are now all releasing tool-capable, reasoning-capable models within weeks of each other, trading benchmark leadership on a monthly cadence. The essay predicted a 3-9 month gap between top US labs; actual performance is compressing toward 0-2 months. The race is tighter than the essay projected. Prediction affected: _q17-us-lab-gap_.

### June 2025: The Government Moves Eighteen Months Early

**Pentagon awards $200M AI contracts to all four frontier labs** In June and July 2025, the US Department of Defense's Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office awarded four separate $200 million ceiling prototype contracts to Anthropic, OpenAI, xAI, and Google for "agentic AI capabilities to support national security." These are two-year other transaction agreements: the government's fast-track contracting mechanism, typically reserved for urgent capability needs. The AI 2027 essay predicted the US government would begin pulling AI companies into a quasi-defense-contractor relationship starting in "early 2027." These contracts represent that relationship beginning in mid-2025, approximately 18 months ahead of the predicted timeline. This is not a small discrepancy; 18 months at current AI development pace is significant. Predictions affected: _q13-dod-ai-contracts_.

**METR evaluates Chinese AI: the gap is real, but it's six months, not twelve** On June 27, METR (Model Evaluation & Threat Research) published evaluation results for mid-2025 DeepSeek and Qwen models. Their finding: "the level of autonomous capabilities of mid-2025 DeepSeek models is similar to the level of capabilities of frontier models from late 2024." In practical terms, Chinese models are approximately six months behind US frontier on agentic task completion. The AI 2027 essay's treatment of China as a near-peer competitor is broadly supported, but the specific gap matters. Six months at a four-to-seven-month doubling rate means Chinese models are meaningfully behind on the capabilities the essay treats as most consequential. The April H20 export controls appear to be having their intended effect, though Qwen3's benchmarks suggest the gap is compressible. Predictions affected: _n22-china-model-gap_, _q8-export-controls_.

**o3-pro and the emerging "think longer" premium tier** OpenAI released o3-pro on June 10: an extended-thinking version of o3 for Pro and Team subscribers, offering more reliable reasoning on hard problems in physics, math, and coding at the cost of longer inference time. This mirrors Anthropic's own premium reasoning approach and suggests that inference scaling (giving models more compute at run-time) is becoming a competitive differentiator alongside training. The essay predicts rapid capability gains from algorithmic improvements; the convergence of OpenAI and Anthropic on extended-thinking premium tiers suggests the two leading labs see the same opportunity. Prediction affected: _q9-continuous-training_.

### May 2025: Coding Agents Ship; the First Level 3 Model Arrives

**Claude Opus 4 triggers ASL-3: the first real-world safety threshold event** On May 22, Anthropic released Claude Opus 4 and simultaneously classified it as the first model to reach ASL-3 under its Responsible Scaling Policy. ASL-3 is defined by Anthropic as the threshold where a model could "provide meaningful uplift to those seeking to create biological, chemical, nuclear, or radiological weapons." This is not a forecast: it's a real-world policy trigger, with concrete security and deployment requirements attached. The AI 2027 essay describes escalating safety thresholds as a central feature of the 2025-2027 arc; Anthropic's ASL-3 designation is the first documented instance of a frontier lab crossing such a threshold with binding operational consequences. Claude Opus 4 also scored 72.5% on SWE-bench Verified: still below the essay's predicted 85% target for mid-2025, but representing the current frontier. Predictions affected: _n17-security-sl3_, _n19-bio-capabilities_, _n14-swebench-85_.

**Coding agents become deployed products** Three events in May mark coding agents reaching deployed product form. OpenAI launched "Codex" on May 15: a cloud-based software engineering agent running on codex-1 (a version of o3) that works asynchronously on multiple tasks in parallel, reading codebases and writing features without supervision. On the same day, Anthropic's Claude Code became generally available after its preview period, with a Code Execution tool, MCP connectors for external tools, and enterprise adoption by Netflix, Spotify, KPMG, L'Oreal, and Salesforce. Google I/O on May 20 added Jules (an async GitHub coding agent) alongside Gemini 2.5 Flash and Project Astra updates. Taken together, May 2025 may mark the month when "AI coding agent" became a mainstream enterprise product category rather than a lab experiment. Anthropic reported 5.5× revenue growth for Claude Code by July from the GA launch date. Predictions affected: _q3-coding-agents_, _q2-unreliable-agents_, _q6-ai-for-ai-research_.

**Stargate expands internationally; infrastructure scale is no longer hypothetical** The Stargate $500B US infrastructure project, announced in January 2025, expanded to international soil in May: Nvidia, Cisco, and OpenAI announced plans for a UAE Stargate data center on May 16, formally confirmed May 22 as a 1 GW campus in Abu Dhabi expected to open in 2026. The geopolitical dimension here goes beyond raw compute: Gulf states offer capital access and a potential route for US AI companies to operate outside export control constraints. The essay predicts massive, globally distributed AI infrastructure investment; the UAE announcement is evidence that this buildout is proceeding on multiple fronts simultaneously. Predictions affected: _q1-infra-investment_, _q7-datacenter-buildout_, _n7-capex-trillion_.

**Dario Amodei on labor displacement** On May 28, Anthropic's CEO told Axios that AI could eliminate half of all entry-level white-collar jobs and spike unemployment to 20% within one to five years: "as little as a couple of years or less." Although CEOs speaking to press routinely compress timelines, the statement is notable directional evidence: the CEO of the lab building some of the most capable AI systems is stating publicly that labor displacement is near-term and large-scale. The essay predicts visible junior developer displacement in 2026; Amodei's statement reflects the same model of how AI value accumulates from the bottom of the skill distribution upward. Prediction affected: _n8-labor-market_.

### April 2025: The Essay Drops Into a Live Experiment

**AI 2027 publishes; the tracker begins responding** Daniel Kokotajlo, Scott Alexander, Eli Lifland, Thomas Larsen, and Romeo Dean published "AI 2027" on April 3, with Scott Alexander's introduction on Astral Codex Ten the same day. This tracker is a direct response to that essay: an ongoing attempt to test its specific predictions against the record. The reception in April was telling: enthusiastic in rationalist and EA circles (Zvi Mowshowitz called it "a serious attempt to write down what the future holds"; LessWrong ran sustained discussion threads), skeptical or ignored outside them. One early counterpoint: FutureSearch subscriber data suggested the essay had forecast 27M ChatGPT paid subscribers when the actual April figure was closer to 20M: a modest but real calibration miss in the short-term numbers.

**OpenAI closes $40B at $300B valuation; o3 and o4-mini launch with tool use** Two events in April are most directly relevant to the essay's infrastructure and agency predictions. OpenAI finalized a $40 billion funding round on April 1, bringing its valuation to $300 billion, nearly double its valuation of six months prior, with active ChatGPT users reported at 500 million weekly. Then on April 16, OpenAI released o3 and o4-mini: reasoning models with native agentic tool use, including web search and code execution during inference. o4-mini reached free-tier availability immediately. These releases are directional evidence that reasoning-capable, tool-using models are arriving on roughly the expected schedule. They do not prove the "2025 is the year of agents" framing. Predictions affected: _q1-infra-investment_, _q3-coding-agents_, _n28-lab-valuation_.

**H20 export controls tightened; open-source models push back on the US-China framing** On April 9, the US government imposed an indefinite export license requirement on Nvidia's H20 chips to China, citing supercomputer risk. Nvidia disclosed $5.5 billion in anticipated charges. This is exactly the kind of compute-access constraint the essay describes as central to US-China AI competition. But the same week, Meta released Llama 4 (Scout, Maverick, Behemoth preview) under Apache 2.0, and Alibaba's Qwen3 family followed on April 28: a 235B-parameter MoE model with benchmark scores competitive with closed frontier models. The picture is mixed: US export controls are real and biting, but China's open-source AI ecosystem is not standing still. Predictions affected: _q8-export-controls_, _n21-china-chip-gap_, _q17-us-lab-gap_.

**Anthropic launches Claude Max; agent pricing arrives where the essay predicted** Anthropic launched "Claude Max" in April at $100/month (5× usage) and $200/month (20× usage). Combined with ChatGPT Pro at $200/month, the premium AI agent tier is now priced exactly where the essay predicted: "hundreds of dollars per month." This is one of the essay's more specific near-term claims, and it was confirmed almost immediately. Prediction affected: _q11-agent-pricing_.

- [Google Lets Engineers Use Rival's Claude Opus 5](https://lumichats.com/blog/google-engineers-claude-opus-5-antigravity-gemini-2026)
Google now gives every engineer a personal quota to use Anthropic's Claude Opus 5 inside its Antigravity platform, even as Gemini stays default.
- [NYSE Used Anthropic's 'Too Dangerous' AI on Itself](https://lumichats.com/blog/anthropic-project-glasswing-mythos-5-1-update-2026)
NYSE told Congress it used Anthropic's Project Glasswing AI to fix bugs, as Checkmarx joins and Mythos 5.1 launches this September.
- [Fable 5.1 Cuts Cache Costs 75%, Adds Free Security](https://lumichats.com/blog/claude-fable-5-1-mythos-5-1-cache-pricing-cut)
Anthropic cut Fable 5.1 cache-read pricing 75% and added free enterprise security. What it means for AI costs and data privacy.
- [Run a Real AI Agent on Your Own GPU](https://lumichats.com/blog/meta-muse-glimmer-open-agent-model-local-gpu-2026)
Meta's new open Muse Glimmer runs agentic tasks locally on one consumer GPU - offline, free, private. What it can and can't do.
- [ChatGPT Free Just Got Unlimited Chats](https://lumichats.com/blog/chatgpt-free-unlimited-chats-think-button-2026)
OpenAI dropped the message cap on free ChatGPT and added a Think button. What's actually unlimited, what still isn't, and the catch.
- [Claude Opus 5: Better Model, Same $20 Plan](https://lumichats.com/blog/claude-opus-5-launch-2026-effort-control-pricing)
Anthropic shipped Opus 5 on July 24. It is the top model on Claude Pro at no price change, plus an effort setting that trades cost for capability.
- [ChatGPT Work Is Here — and GPT-5.6 Just Went Public](https://lumichats.com/blog/chatgpt-work-openai-super-app-gpt-5-6-public-2026)
OpenAI launched ChatGPT Work, an agentic 'super app', and released GPT-5.6 to everyone after a 12-day government hold. What it does, and the catch.
- [OpenAI Finished GPT-5.6. Washington Won't Let You Use It Yet.](https://lumichats.com/blog/gpt-5-6-sol-terra-luna-government-restricted-2026)
OpenAI's GPT-5.6 shipped to just 20 government-approved partners over security concerns. What Sol, Terra and Luna do, and when you can use them.
- [ChatGPT Plus vs Claude Pro 2026: Should You Still Pay $20/Month? The Honest Answer](https://lumichats.com/blog/chatgpt-plus-vs-claude-pro-2026-should-you-cancel-honest-comparison-free-alternatives)
Meta just released one of the top 5 AI models in the world for free. Gemini 3.1 Pro ties GPT-5.4 for #1 on independent benchmarks and is accessible free. So why are you still paying $20/month? We ran a 6-week head-to-head test of ChatGPT Plus and Claude Pro across coding, writing, research, and daily tasks. Here is who wins, who loses, and the specific situations where free AI is now genuinely good enough.
- [You're Using the Wrong AI Model: A 2-Minute Test to Fix It](https://lumichats.com/blog/wrong-ai-model-2026-find-the-right-one-for-your-work)
Most people pick ChatGPT and use it for everything — exactly like using a hammer for every home repair. In 2026, GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Perplexity, and Meta AI have measurably different strengths for measurably different tasks. Claude leads SWE-bench software engineering and produces human-quality writing. Gemini has a 2M token context window and live Google Search. GPT leads computer use, structured outputs, and image generation. This is the complete task-by-task routing guide — with a 60-second diagnostic test — for finding the AI model that is actually right for your specific work.
- [AI Is Fighting America's Wars: OpenAI and the Pentagon](https://lumichats.com/blog/ai-iran-war-2026-pentagon-openai-anthropic-what-is-really-happening)
OpenAI signed a defense contract. Anthropic — the company founded on AI safety — was described as 'turbocharging US strikes on Iran' by MIT Technology Review. The QuitGPT movement exploded. London saw the largest AI protest in history. Claude briefly hit #1 in the US App Store as people deleted ChatGPT. And most of the Americans using these tools every day still don't know any of this happened. This is the complete, honest account of how the AI companies you use entered America's wars — and what it means for the tools, the companies, and the conversation we should be having.
- [What Is MCP? The Protocol That Lets AI Talk to Everything](https://lumichats.com/blog/what-is-mcp-model-context-protocol-complete-guide-2026)
MCP is the most important AI infrastructure standard you have never heard of — until now. Created by Anthropic, adopted by OpenAI and Google, it has over 6,400 servers and is the backbone of every serious AI agent in 2026. This is the complete plain-English guide: what MCP is, why it matters, how it works, and how students and developers can use it today.
- [OpenAI o3 and o4-mini: What Reasoning Models Actually Do](https://lumichats.com/blog/openai-o3-reasoning-models-explained-plain-english-guide-2026)
OpenAI's o3 scored 87.5% on ARC-AGI-1 — tasks designed to be impossible for AI. o4-mini matches it at a fraction of the cost. Google's Gemini 2.5 Pro scored 77.1% on ARC-AGI-2. These are not regular AI models — they think before answering. This complete guide explains what reasoning models actually are, how they differ from GPT-5.4 and Claude, when to use them, and what the benchmarks actually mean.
- [OpenAI $25B, Anthropic $19B: The Real AI Industry in 2026](https://lumichats.com/blog/openai-anthropic-ai-industry-reality-check-2026-usa)
OpenAI has surpassed $25 billion in annualized revenue and is moving toward an IPO. Anthropic is approaching $19 billion. The AI industry has become one of the fastest-growing technology sectors ever. But between the headlines and the hype is a more complex picture. This is the honest state of AI in America in 2026.
- [AGI Timeline Predictions 2026: Why Experts Clash](https://lumichats.com/blog/agi-timeline-2026-expert-predictions-what-it-means)
Anthropic: late 2026. Metaculus: February 2028. OpenAI says it already knows how. LeCun says transformers cannot. Why all four can be right.

### What changed since 2024

Dealroom’s May 2024 report on the Magnificent 7 said major acquisitions were “basically off the table” under regulatory scrutiny, and that the seven were dominating venture rounds instead. The first half of that no longer holds: they bought 26 companies in 2026, against 56 in 2013, but at prices a decade ago would not have cleared.

PNG

# Twelve Magnificent 7 acquisitions above $1bn since 2024

Each tile is one deal, sized by price and coloured by which of the seven bought it.

AlphabetNvidiaAmazonMetaAppleTesla

$32bn’25$20bn’25$14.3bn’25Hugging Face$12.9bn’26$11.6bn’26$4.8bn$2.7bn$2.4bn$2bnDensity AIMechanizeQ.ai

Source: **Dealroom.co** · Meta’s Scale purchase was a 49% stake

### What this means

The concentration is in the dollars, not the deals. Four rounds carry $237 billion of this year’s $308 billion, so the 45% figure describes a handful of AI companies raising at a scale nobody else can match, financed in large part by the firms that also sell them compute.

Underneath that, the seven are diverging. Alphabet runs the largest venture operation of any company in the world, across sixteen vehicles, and still leads on deal count. Nvidia built one from almost nothing in three years and now deploys the most money. Amazon has held flat on deal count. Microsoft’s has more than halved since 2021, even as it wrote the single largest cheques. Apple, Meta and Tesla are not really in this business.

And the acquisition freeze has ended. Alphabet bought Wiz for $32 billion, Nvidia bought Groq for $20 billion and Hugging Face for $12.9 billion, Amazon bought Globalstar for $11.6 billion.

[NVIDIA now joins more $100M+ VC rounds than any investor \| Dealroom](https://dealroom.co/resources/nvidia-megaround-investor/)

NVIDIA's quarterly filing for the period to 26 July 2026 values its
equity investments at $99B, up from about $7B a year earlier. The filing says what the stakes are worth. Dealroom's funding data shows where the activity went, counted as rounds joined rather than money invested.


Dealroom records which investors took part in a round and the round's total size, not how the total splits between them. NVIDIA was one of nine investors in OpenAI's $122B round, and only NVIDIA's own disclosure says its share was $30B. Where a cheque is known it is marked as NVIDIA's figure; everywhere else the number is the round. NVIDIA here includes NVentures, its venture arm, and 2026 runs from January to August.


Start with every round NVIDIA has joined. Counting rounds of every size, NVIDIA took part in 88 venture rounds between January and 8 September 2026, against 86 in all of 2025 and 26 in 2021. At the 2026 pace the year ends near 128.

What the companies sell shows where the money sits in the stack. Of the 53 rounds, 19 went to companies that train models, 12 to companies that sell GPU capacity or run models for others, 6 to chip, networking and data-centre power companies, and 11 to makers of robots and autonomous vehicles. 5 went to companies that apply AI to law, materials, engineering and healthcare. The first four layers sit between the chip and the end user; only the application companies sell to businesses outside the AI industry, and together they raised $1.8B of the $205B.

### What this means

NVIDIA sits on the cap tables of many of the companies that buy its
chips. The 53 megarounds it joined in eight months put it ahead of
every venture firm, and the portfolio it reports is worth $99B. A
founder raising $100M or more in 2026 was more likely to have NVIDIA
in the round than Sequoia.


For venture firms the change is in who they share their largest
rounds with. The investor present in the most $100M+ rounds is no longer a fund but a supplier to the companies being funded, and its
stake in a round comes with the chips those companies need to spend
the money on.
